speakeroldname: Hon. Brooke Claxton (Minister of National Defence):
maintopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY MEMBER FOR WINNIPEG SOUTH CENTRE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last night the member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) made a number of statements, and he expressly asked me to give certain assurances. Because of the nature of those statements and their possible effect on the forces abroad and their families at home, I felt that in the national interest I should make an immediate statement. Accordingly, I have delayed my departure abroad, and if I have the unanimous consent of the house, I shall proceed to make a statement now. It will not be long.
I refer to that part of the hon. member's speech in which the impression is created that the rate of casualties suffered is, in any way whatever, comparable to those at Dieppe. Whilst this may not have been the intention of the hon. member, you can see the impression created by the reference in the dispatch as it appears in this morning's Montreal Gazette. It reads:
The Winnipeg soldier M.P. warned that to date Canadian casualties in Korea had been about 60 per cent-"the same heavy casualties rate as at Dieppe".
At Dieppe, of forces numbering 4,963, 3,371 were casualties in eight hours. In Korea the 25th Canadian infantry brigade have been there a total of 7,900 man years. The total number of casualties suffered numbers 1,248 or 16 per cent as opposed to the 68 per cent in eight hours at Dieppe. It must be remembered and emphasized that the 25th Canadian infantry brigade is practically all in the active theatre of operations in front of brigade headquarters. I am informed by the chief of the general staff that the casualty rate of the 25th brigade, as related to the actions in which they have been engaged, has been lower than any comparable formation in the war in Korea or in the second world war, and that has been due to the finest possible equipment, good training, maintenance of strength and good leadership. The fact that so far the brigade has only lost one prisoner of war is a remarkable tribute to its fighting quality and fighting spirit.
The care that casualties receive is shown by the fact that of the non-fatal battle casualties less than 3 per cent died of wounds while the figure was 6 per cent in the second world war and 8 [DOT] 1 per cent in the first world war.
So far as ammunition is concerned, the position in Korea is precisely as I outlined it the other day. Canadian troops have never been subjected to unnecessary casualties by any shortage of ammunition, nor are they in the least likely to be exposed in such a manner. The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that the amount of ammunition used in Korea far exceeds that ever used before in any campaign in the history of mankind for any force of a comparable size. During quiet periods ammunition is conserved, on precisely the same basis for the Canadians as for the other forces, against the possibility of attack and to maintain an essential theatre reserve against contingencies. If an armistice is agreed on it might well include a condition, that there should be no supplementing of military formations or stores in the theatre while it is in force. If an armistice is agreed on such terms and fighting should subsequently break out again, the forces would have placed themselves in a position of unjustifiable risk had they not provided for theatre stocks.
As for the political and superior military control of the Canadian forces, we have a position in the commonwealth division and in the army appropriate to our position as having: the third largest fighting force among the United Nations in Korea.
The brigade commander may, either through the usual channels or direct, bring to attention any situation in which he feels that Canadian lives would be needlessly risked, or any other circumstances requiring attention, in Korea, in Japan and, if necessary, at Washington. The brigade commander is specifically given the right of direct communication to the chief of the general staff in Ottawa on any matter and can call for representation to be made to the United Nations command either through military or governmental channels in the event that he should feel that he was required to take any action which involved the acceptance of unjustifiable military risks to his troops. Happily, no situation has arisen necessitating such an appeal, and with the confidence which we may feel in the calibre of the command in the theatre such an appeal is not to be expected.

NATO Conference
I am sure that the hon. member did not intend his remarks to be harmful to the magnificent spirit of our fighting forces and I am sure he did not want to cause additional distress and concern to their wives and mothers at home here in Canada.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am sure that the minister would not care to have one of his statements misinterpreted this afternoon. As I heard it, I think he was suggesting that I had not drawn a careful distinction between the casualties at Dieppe which were suffered over a period of a few hours and the casualties suffered by the 25th brigade over a period of 22 months. I was extremely careful to note the time element involved in those two cases.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in view of the minister's desire to remove any uncertainties before he leaves, may I ask him if he will inform the house whether the statement conveyed to the people of Canada by the Canadian Press yesterday, and which informed the Canadian people as to the attitude that he and Ihe members of his party are to take at the 'NATO meetings, does in fact represent the position of the government, in view of the fact that the statement was said to come from ^responsible authorities?

speakeroldname: Hon. Brooke Claxton (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: PRESS REPORT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am in no way responsible for what the newspapers print. When I make statements, I am glad to have them printed as I make them. Yesterday I made a statement in answer to the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) which I think covers the situation completely. Canada entered into the North Atlantic treaty in good faith. She has formed a partnership for the preservation of peace. We have already taken part in every meeting of the council and have made the commitments which I have reported to this house. We will consider with our other fellow members everything brought before us that is likely to strengthen the forces which we are building up to prevent aggression and to preserve peace. I will not make any commitment abroad because that would not be in accordance with our constitutional practice, but I will be glad to participate in discussions and to exchange views freely and fully with my colleagues, most of whom I know well. Then I will make a report to the government.

subtopic: COMMENT ON STATEMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: The hon. member was kind enough to send me a copy of the St. John's paper. NAFEL is the single marketing agency for export of fish from Newfoundland, which was set up under the commission form of government prior to Newfoundland entering confederation, and, as one of the terms of union with Canada, was allowed to be carried over to the spring of 1954. The statement made by the Secretary of State is quite right. In the forthcoming year very serious consideration will be given by the Department of Fisheries and the provincial government in consultation with the fishing industry and the fishermen as to what course will be taken when the present agreement lapses. When a decision is taken it will be announced in this house.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire for a very short time to give some attention to the excellent speeches of the hon. members, respectively, for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Deslieres) and Waterloo North (Mr. Schneider), whose speeches inaugurated the present debate. I was particularly interested in the case made by the hon. member for Waterloo North on behalf of those very unfortunate people, the blind of this country. I think it is a great credit to the House of Commons that a man whose name for many years has been associated with the larger industrialization of this country should have made such a plea. For

The Address-Mr. Laing myself, I consider it an excellent omen for the continued vitality of the party to which both he and I belong.
Mr. Speaker, I must make reference to the recent appointments to the cabinet from British Columbia. We were delighted in British Columbia-and I say that all the people of that province were delighted-when the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair) was appointed to the post of Minister of Fisheries. And we were doubly delighted when the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Campney) was appointed to the post of Solicitor General. We in British Columbia interpret these appointments as indicating that some attention is being paid by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and his government to the growing strength and the growing responsibility of British Columbia within this nation. But, more than that we are sure these two members will bring new strength and new lustre to the wider councils of the nation.
I should like also to refer to the former minister of fisheries for the Dominion of Canada, who has gone to a new and onerous task as Canada's first post-war ambassador to Japan. We in British Columbia, whose windows look out upon the Pacific, have for many years been deeply concerned over the contraction of trade in that general area. In a world which is increasing its population at the rate of 60,000 souls per day, one-half of all the world's population lives on the rim of the Pacific.
There was a time when we had the great white Empresses, and the ships of other lines, running regularly across the Pacific. But in recent years these have disappeared. We were happy in British Columbia when the Canadian Pacific Railway took two of its better freight ships recently and put them on that run. But we in that province earnestly hope that the re-establishment of Japanese trade will be used as a springboard for the resumption of trade all around the Pacific. And I am going to say this, that of all the people who have been in the public service of this country we could not have appointed to that post a more able and more deeply versed businessman than Mr. Mayhew.
Mr. Speaker, I have one or two local problems associated with my own city with which I should like to deal first; and the first of these has to do with the Vancouver international airport. I was a little surprised the other day when the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) brought up the matter of the connecting link between the city and the airport. With one part of his assertion I agree entirely, and that 

is as to the importance of our Vancouver international airport. With the single exception of the item of air mail, our Vancouver international airport is today the greatest in the Dominion of Canada, and it is shortly going to be one of the greatest airports on this continent. In the matter of passengers it is today handling 1,700 per day. It is handling a higher weight of air freight than any other airport in Canada. It was established in 1929 as a city airport, and has grown markedly every year since that time. Out of it travel all the Trans-Canada Air Lines and United Air Lines service to the United States, as well as the service of Canadian Pacific Air Lines across the Pacific. And there is now being inaugurated service to South America and to the Antipodes. It is a great airport.
But the other evening the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra dealt with it as if the only important matter were the connecting link. Well, I have been the member for Vancouver South since 1949. I know however that before that the hon. member who is now the member for Vancouver-Quadra represented Vancouver South. I have searched in vain for anything he said, prior to 1949, in reference either to the airport or to the connecting link.
It is true that the connecting link is not a good one. We refer to it as the Marpole bridge. I do not think the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra knows that the first bridge was built there prior to 1890 and that there have been no fewer than four re-establishments of bridges at that location since. The last bridge was built in 1927 at a cost of $275,000.
At the present time the bridge is carrying over 18,000 vehicles per day, a fact which I think is a great tribute to British Columbia lumber and British Columbia pilings capable of carrying that weight for that amount of money.
This bridge is 100 per cent the responsibility of the provincial government, because it was taken over by a bill which passed the British Columbia legislature. The hon. member referred to negotiations which had been undertaken between the federal government and the city of Vancouver for the acquisition of the airport. After all, I would remind him that even in the city of Vancouver it takes two to make a bargain. The federal administration and the Department of Transport have repeatedly done their level best to come to some agreement in respect of the purchase of that airport where, today, for every dollar invested by the city the government of Canada has at least twenty.

There were and there still are on the city-council in Vancouver some members who think that the airport is a goose which will lay golden eggs, and that the city should retain it. I am not of that opinion because I think that, from the very nature of the airport, the cost should be visited upon the widest possible taxation basis, and that is all the people of Canada. I would suggest to him that in the ensuing months we may have an opportunity of reopening with the city council of Vancouver the question of the acquisition of the airport, and I know that any help he will be able to give us at that time will be deeply appreciated. It will then be soon enough for us to consider a contribution by the federal administration toward the cost of improvements and increased facilities at that airport.

We are assured by -people in Vancouver that during the current year they will ship not less than 125 million bushels, which would give us a factor of over six bushels. Vancouver is an all-year port
The Address-Mr. Laing and we have advantages which are denied to other ports in Canada where storage facilities are located.
In addition to that we are strategically located, and this refers also to that great and growing port of Prince Rupert. As a result, during recent years considerable shipments of United States grain have been made through Vancouver from the great area in Washington state. There have been other shipments of United States corn for partial storage. Because of the situation existing on the Pacific, in the eventuality of that tragedy which we all fear, the dispersal of this grain is of great advantage to those people who are on our side.

I leave this matter with the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) in the hope that he or the wheat board will find some way to increase this capacity. I think it could well be increased at this time by not less than ten million bushels.
I was delighted yesterday to hear the speech delivered in this house by the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll). I want to take my place beside him in asking for a parliamentary committee to investigate every aspect of a national system of health insurance. I do that because I cannot support the subamendment introduced by the leader of the C.C.F. (Mr. Coldwell); for implicit in that subamendment is the thought that we can embark immediately upon a system of national health insurance.
I want to say at the start that I have no confidence in state medicine, which has been so construed in some countries and which it has been attempted to put into operation in others. I want no system that will interfere with the normal relation that exists between patient and doctor. But I do want, as soon as we can bring it about in this country, a system that will place the responsibility for illness, accident, incapacity and ill health upon all the people of the country instead of upon those unfortunates who happen to be in that position.
This is a problem of tremendous area. It is a problem whose horizons are forever receding. I was interested recently in reading some material put out by some medical men who point out that recent studies in endocrinology and the use of antibiotics may well increase longevity by another ten years by the end of this century. That would have a tremendous influence upon the whole problem and I believe that the eventual action that will have to be taken will be indicated

The Address-Mr. Laing more clearly if we appoint a committee at once to make the broadest possible inquiries in every sphere.
The social services which we now have in Canada are more generous than those of any nation on the face of the earth having regard to our population. I was interested in an article which appeared in the December 5 issue of U. S. News and World Report entitled "Pay-As-You-Go Social Security" and subheaded "The Plan: Today's Benefits from Today's Taxes." The article reads:
A new plan, favoured by a growing number of businessmen and business organizations, calls for an end to the idea of a multibillion-dollar social security reserve fund. Payroll taxes, instead, would be levied only as needed to finance pensions for all on a pay-as-you-go basis.
Which is the very plan that we decided upon recently in Canada. Here is a further indication of the generosity of the Canadian system:
Retired workers, aged 65 or more, who now are not eligible for pensions will start to draw monthly benefits of $25 to $35 a month. Their wives, if 65 or over, will draw half that much.
In the realm of old age pensions, old age insurance, veterans pensions, veterans allowances and family allowances, we are paying something in excess of one billion dollars. If we add to that the cost of the health plans upon which we have embarked we find we are paying one and a quarter billion dollars annually. I think we have in Canada today the most enlightened and most generous plans in the way of social security. Notwithstanding that, I am prepared to support the hon. member for Spadina in the very excellent presentation he made yesterday.
I want for a few moments to deal with some matters of trade, and with particular reference to the attitude that is apparently growing among members of the official opposition. During the last interlude between our sessional sittings we had visits to the city of Vancouver by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) and the leader of the C.C.F. group (Mr. Coldwell). Both of them received a resounding Vancouver welcome. That is to be expected because all the girls love to be courted even though the swain is ineligible. Somebody behind me says we had a visit from the Prime Minister. Yes, we did. We had a visit from the Prime Minister, and I detract nothing from my references to the other two hon. members when I say I think the Prime Minister was the most sincerely and deeply loved of them all.
I was particularly interested in certain comments made by the Leader of the Opposition in his Vancouver speech to which I

listened. It took me back to the days of 1949 when there was circulated within our province a piece of Tory propaganda which started out by saying "lost". They told the people of British Columbia that all the markets for lumber had been lost, all the markets for fish had been lost, and all the markets for apples had been lost. They said we had lost everything. This propaganda was printed on white paper in Tory blue, and the contents were bluer and more pessimistic than the ink. I have some of it here. This is the material that was put out for Progressive Conservative speakers in 1949-"lost, lost, lost, lost". Well, we are hearing it all over again.

We heard it all over again in Vancouver. The Leader of the Opposition had been in the United Kingdom a short time previously and when he said to his audience in Vancouver that we want to re-establish contacts with the mother country he was speaking to a receptive audience, and he knew it. There is great thought, there is great hope in our province for the mother country. He said it was not good enough to say that we could not conduct business between the United Kingdom and Canada. He said that if a trigger-happy Russian soldier were to start a third world war we would find a way in two weeks. Of course we would find a way. We would find the identical way we found in the last war, by loans and gifts, because I am now convinced that all of us on the free side of the world will quickly act as firemen if a fire starts in the house of any one of us.
But what contribution is that to the idea of trade, not aid? We want something better than that. As a matter of fact I never expected to hear such a comment in our city from the leader of the Conservative party. We have been hearing that kind of stuff for years from the leaders of the provincial group of the C.C.F. party. We have been hearing that we will not have any prosperity unless we get involved in a capitalistic war. That is what the C.C.F. provincial leadership has been telling us for a long time. Well, we are going 'to have trade and not aid. The very nature of trade makes it a two-way street, and I think that is a fact that has been lost on the members of the Conservative party in this house. We cannot bring meat from England. They eat meat but they do not produce it. They have no wheat. They import wheat. If we are going to trade with the United Kingdom we must be prepared to take the things that they are best adapted to give us, textiles.

I want to quote certain remarks of the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Blair), a man for whom I have the greatest respect. On March 7, 1952, he stated in the house that Great Britain is the chief exporter of woollen goods to Canada, and has now obtained an increasing share of our domestic market amounting to 86 per cent of all imports. He also said, as found at page 209 of Hansard:
A great percentage of the wool fabrics that have been imported into Canada came from Great Britain, and there is no control or restriction on the volume of these imports.
Trade, not aid; but as soon as the old mother country sends us the things that she is most capable of giving us we raise once again the cry that once resounded in this house, tariffs as high as Haman's gallows.
I was most interested in a speech made in the house the other night by the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy) dealing with sugar and tobacco. He wants neither sugar nor tobacco brought into this country but ample protection given for Canadian production of both. In that he is joined by the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore), who advised me yesterday that he wanted some protection for sugar, and he is going to let me know how much at a later date. The hon. member for Lambton West had a great deal to say about sugar, and there was another time when he had a great deal to say about the cost of living in this country. In the house on February 8, 1951, when the cry of the Tory party was that the government had better get busy and do something about inflation and the rising cost of living, the hon. member for Lambton West had this to say, as found at page 189 of Hansard:
It is the story of the housewife in Sarnia and in Ottawa, in Winnipeg and in Vancouver, who daily is fighting a losing battle against the rising cost of living. And for the housewife with a family of small children it is a bitter struggle as the household dollar shrinks to the point where food has to be sacrificed in order to buy clothes, or clothes have to be sacrificed in order that enough can be provided the family to eat. Here again the federal government stubbornly refuses to translate into action facts as they exist.
He was full of tears that night for the consumers of Canada. As the result of actions of this government, what has happened to prices? I now wish to refer to the Toronto Star of November 22, 1952, with respect to what prices are doing. Sugar was $10.30 a hundred pounds in November, 1951, and it is now $8.60. Does the hon. member for Lambton West deplore the fact that sugar has come down from $10.30 to $8.60? Does he want it to be protected so that it will go back from $8.60 to $10.30?

To what an admirable degree we are doing just that today. We are using those resources for the benefit of the people of Canada. My hon. friend says "Don't you?". The hon. member quoted Mr. Ash, president of the Shell Oil Company, and recommended that gentleman's speech to the provinces of Alberta and British Columbia. The hon. member was in favour of the immediate export of both gas and oil from his

The Address-Mr. Laing province. There is nothing very consistent about the whole plan. The arrows point nowhere.
I come now to iron ore. I am sorry the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) is not in his seat. We are exporting iron ore from British Columbia to Japan at the rate of about 100,000 tons per month. The hon. member has called it a scandal and a disgrace. What is the situation with respect to that iron ore? The Japanese came out of the conflict with a steel capacity of about 10 million tons. It was decided by the people on our side that it was imperative that that capacity be used to its full extent. Japan formerly drew its ore from Korea and the mainland, and with that source entirely cut off they are taking iron ore from British Columbia today on a basis that is not economic. They are paying $8 or $8.50 a ton for the ore and they are paying over $12 a ton for the freight. The United States, which our friends see as a dangerous country to deal with and a country of which we should beware, is subsidizing the economy of Japan to the extent of $700 million annually to keep Japan out of the sphere of red China.
Unless we make a study of our position, I do not see how we can have a policy in this country in respect to trade. The hit and miss style I have heard coming from the other side I think might well place Canada, if these people came to power, in one of the most dangerous positions in which Canada has ever been.
Today trade is difficult. It is based fundamentally on conciliation, and if you are going to say to someone, "Keep your goods, we will not buy them but we demand a market for ours," then this trade situation which is very critical in the world today could be delivered into disaster.

Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the mover, (Mr. Deslieres) and the seconder (Mr. Schneider) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Their speeches were well prepared and well delivered. It is my intention today to devote my time to a discussion of the subamendment moved by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). The subamendment reads as follows:
We regret further that Your Excellency's advisers have failed: (a) To recommend legislation establishing a nation-wide health insurance program, with provision for provincial administration; (b) to implement their proposals to the dominion-provincial conference of 1945.
It is my hope, Mr. Speaker, that this matter will be freely debated in this house and that all members will express their opinions concerning a question of such vital importance.
During the time that I have been a member of this house I have advocated a plan of health insurance and in consideration of statistics involving mortality rates, incidence of disease, hospital accommodation, preventive measures and other considerations relating to this subject, I have frequently expressed impatience that we were not proceeding more rapidly to a solution of a matter so vital to our nation.
I regard this subject as of such grave importance that I hope there will be in no way any political shadow-boxing either in this chamber or in the forthcoming general elections. There is no doubt of the necessity of additional health measures, but we must have a clear understanding of the whole situation

The Address-Mr. Blair and the measures necessary to remedy and to correct inadequacies of our present situation.
It is a trait of human nature that man should be concerned about the physical wellbeing of his family; and there exists in the mind of every citizen the fear of sickness and suffering in his immediate circle. Sickness or accident may invade any member of the family-the breadwinner, the mother or the children.' But when for financial reasons medical services cannot be secured, the fear becomes intensified and becomes a matter of constant worry. The consideration of health services should not be a dull routine discussion in the House of Commons. Serious consideration to measures which would give proper assurance against the recurring fear of uncertainty in the ability of all citizens to obtain adequate treatment should be the concern of any government that has regard for the happiness of the people.
The most important asset of any country is its people. There can be only one sound foundation upon which a happy and prosperous nation can be built, namely, the good health of its members. This should be the primary concern of government. The ultimate objective of various departments of health should be to bring to everyone an equal opportunity to attain physical and mental health regardless of race, economic status or geographical position.
There are certain factors that are necessary to a proper health program. I place these factors as follows: One, sufficient hospitals and other institutions concerned with the care of those members of the nation who are ill; two, sufficient doctors, nurses, and trained personnel to carry out a full and complete program; three, diagnostic and preventive facilities; four, research; five, an educational program in order that the plan may receive the support of the public; six and last, but most important, government aid and direction.
The position in which we find ourselves in Canada is not one that we can view with complacency regarding our national health. Much has been accomplished, but much remains to be done before we can feel satisfied that we have corrected all existing deficiencies.
Let us give consideration to our present situation. The cost of medical care has increased tremendously in the past twenty years, as new methods of diagnosis and treatment have been discovered. However, these new methods of diagnosis have resulted in the successful treatment of diseases that were formerly considered incurable. The

costs of medical services are increasing, but the ability of the people to pay for these services has not increased.
Medical science is making great strides, but the application of some of those discoveries has not been made available to all our people. It is the duty of the community and of the state to care for the unfortunate who are unable to seek and procure proper attention. It is unfortunate that people in the lower salaries who formerly were able to pay are no longer able to do so on account of the high and increasing costs of hospitalization and treatment. Even in the most severe illnesses, they cannot afford the necessities such as special nurses and hospital service. Unless an illness is acute, these people are forced to neglect chronic conditions for financial reasons.
Family allowances have done much for children, but it is regrettable that children belonging to those families cannot have defects corrected at a time when such correction would be of most benefit to them. It is most important that we develop good citizens in Canada, since the future of the nation depends on the physical, mental and moral health of our youth. The necessity of the physical health of our young men was brought sharply to our attention during the last war when over 40 per cent of our young men did not measure up to the required standards at the time of enlistment.
At this point, Mr. Speaker, I wish to pay a tribute to those serving on boards of hospital administration throughout Canada. Faced with mounting costs of maintenance, and almost prohibitive costs of new construction, they have endeavoured to meet those additional expenses and provide accommodation for their patients at a daily rate as low as possible. In this they have not been successful. The costs to the patients have risen to a point where sickness is getting beyond the financial meang of the average citizen.
In view of the marked shortage of beds in some areas, it has been necessary to place patients on a waiting list for weeks and even months. I pay tribute to the staffs of the hospitals, and especially to the doctors, both in their practices in and outside hospitals. To their credit let it be said that they have not hesitated to give freely of their service without recompense. I especially mention the general practitioners, who made it a point of pride that no cases requiring attention should go unattended.

It should be pointed out that while doctors charge their patients who can pay, they also provide free attention to those who cannot pay. Unfortunately the public does not give the doctor credit for the large amount of service given gratis.
There are few hospitals which do not have a deficit at the end of each financial year. Often hospital boards attempt to make up this deficit by an appeal for voluntary support. Both in the financial help required and in the number of appeals in the past few years, it is doubtful whether the general public can satisfy this need, in view of the higher living costs and higher taxes. The heavy expenses incurred by hospitals, and to which these deficits are accountable, are largely in providing public ward accommodation and diagnostic services, in addition to the general costs of maintenance of the whole hospital. This places a heavy burden on the patient who pays for private or semiprivate rooms. While considering hospital costs and accommodation, we must mention the number of chronic cases occupying beds which could very well be used for the treatment of acute cases. Unfortunately, there is very little in the way of hospitals in Canada for chronic cases. General hospitals in most areas are the only accommodation. These patients occupy active treatment beds for long periods at considerable expense, and cause a shortage of hospital beds for acute cases. The shortage of hospital beds exists in many provinces in spite of hospital grants as in Ontario, my own province, where the province and the dominion both give grants for new hospital construction on a rate per bed. But even with these grants, rising construction costs overcome the grants and these grants, while a help, are insufficient.
It is true that the federal government has made grants toward construction of a large number of hospital beds since the introduction of the health plans in 1948. These grants amount to $1,000 per bed for acute cases, and $1,500 per bed for chronic cases. When the late prime minister, Mr. King, introduced health grants in the House of Commons he said, as reported in Hansard of May, 1948, at page 3934:
The proposed hospital construction grants represent only a portion of the costs of hospital construction. The balance will have to be met by provincial grants and by local funds from other sources.
There has been a sharp rise in building costs since that time. Building costs vary in different areas, but I am informed that in one Ontario city contemplating further hospital extension, the cost per bed has been estimated at $15,000. Allowing for the federal grant and the grant which will come
The Address-Mr. Blair from the province, this will leave a sum of approximately $1,300,000 to be financed by the province and the municipality.
I have mentioned hospitals for chronic cases and the fact that we are faced with a shortage of beds for this type of case. Owing to the introduction of new treatment, our population is increasing in the older age groups.
New treatment is making our population longer-lived. Diseases such as pneumonia, which afflicted so many people in advanced age and rated high in the list of the causes of death, is no longer such a menace. But it is natural that old people should ultimately become afflicted with some form of invalidism requiring institutional care. Not only old people but many in the younger age groups require care for chronic conditions. At present there is a shortage of beds for such cases and they become a problem for the hospitals requiring beds for the acute cases. Cancer cases may be included in this group requiring a long period of hospitalization.
Cancer may be regarded as the greatest problem facing medical research today, and any attack we make on this problem must be a long-term attack. Education must be an important factor. An educational program should emphasize not only early symptoms but ability to procure early treatment.
We must see to it that opportunities for early treatment and diagnosis are made available to every patient. In the last year for which I was able to obtain statistics, 16,258 people in Canada died of this disease. Better and more extensive facilities are required if we are to bring this terrible disease under some semblance of control. But the real tragedy of the fact lies in this, that many of these cases occurred because the disease was not recognized in its early stages, when a cure could have been effected. Although the number of cases of tuberculosis is slowly being lessened, yet we must not believe that a disease which caused over 4,000 deaths in the last year is under control. Not only is hospital care for this disease expensive, but it is a disease of early adult life, and occurs in the most productive age group.
In consideration of the mortality of 4,000 cases in the last year, we must also remember the thousands of people who have been cured, and the fact that this disease is a menace to our population.
We can be proud of our progress in maternal mortality, but our infant mortality rates are much higher as compared with other countries. A high percentage of these deaths occurred in the first month of life. In 1948, the last year for which I was able to obtain

The Address-Mr. Blair statistics, 3,892 babies died because of prematurity. Excellent results have been obtained in handling premature cases, but such care is not available to all mothers. I would draw attention particularly to the rate in the United States as compared with that in Canada.
The number of deaths in Canada of children under five years of age was 17,899. Many of these cases were the result of communicable disease; yet a comparison of several years' statistics shows that there are wide variations between provinces.
[Mr. Blair.)
Several years ago, when I was speaking in 'this chamber regarding our infant mortality rates, I made the statement that these babies were the best immigrants that Canada could procure. They are the descendants of those sturdy people responsible for the building of our nation. Canada can ill afford to lose them.
It is not my purpose to elaborate upon statistics of all mortality rates in diseases, but I have mentioned these for the purpose of showing the further need for action in Canada. I could also mention the high and increasing incidence of mental disease and, again, the shortage of beds for these cases.
According to a recent statement by the bureau of statistics, the number of oases in mental institutions has increased proportionately by nearly 31 per cent in the last twenty years. The first survey since 1931 shows that 394 out of every 100,000 are patients in mental institutions. This shows an increase of 93 from the former figure of 301 per 100,000 registered in the 1931 census. These statistics are disturbing and we must take every means to lower these percentages. Hospital beds must be available, staffed with psychiatrists and trained personnel. Let me summarize our needs as follows:
1.	Hospital beds for-
(a) acute cases; (b) chronic cases; (c) mental illness.
2.	Adequate provision for early diagnosis and early treatment of cancer.
3.	Relief to our people from the high costs of treatment, especially from the high cost of hospitalization.
4.	Extension of program to train more personnel to staff hospitals, especially facilities to provide trained nurses.
5.	Further program to cut down infant and child mortality rate.
If any health plan is undertaken it is essential to have a sufficient number of beds and sufficient personnel trained to carry out such a scheme. To anyone present who is satisfied with our present conditions, let me again refer him to the fact that such a large number of our young men were unfit for service in the last war. During my time in the House of Commons I have almost yearly pleaded for a health plan to overcome these drawbacks to our nation. In 1949 I made the following statement on behalf of the party and the position taken by it. This statement, as reported at page 1154 of Hansard for Friday, March 4, 1949, and which still stands as our policy, is as follows:
This party has long realized the necessity for a plan of health in the Dominion of Canada. Let there be no doubt where this party stands on that

now. We stand in favour of a plan which, in cooperation with the provinces, will give the people the maximum of services, and yet be a plan of freedom, where the doctors will not be civil servants, and which will allow free choice between doctor and patient. We have got a full realization of the deficiencies in treatment services, and we stand ready to implement a plan to overcome these deficiencies, and which will raise health standards in Canada to the equal of that in any other country of the world.
All political parties in this house are committed to health insurance. The Liberal party promised health insurance in 1919. Since that time, they have never at any time suggested that they did not stand by that promise, but on the contrary have reasserted it on a number of occasions. It is appropriate to point out that it would be unfortunate if any promises were made, in addition to those which already have been made, which could not be carried into effect.
The present government placed certain general proposals regarding a national health program before the dominion-provincial conference of 1945. These proposals may be found in the blue book relating to national health insurance, which was placed before that conference. Discussion of that part of the proposals did not proceed in any detail, because the government emphasized the fact that this could not be proceeded with until there was a full and general examination of this problem. That has been the position of the government, and it is for this reason that we have been pressing for some years to have an inquiry of this nature take place, which will provide the basic information without which no satisfactory plan for Canada can be developed.
Health grants were brought into effect in 1948. We gladly voted for these grants on the ground that any money voted for health purposes would help in some degree to cut down mortality and relieve suffering and misery. We felt that in many ways the grants were insufficient and only a stopgap to avoid dealing with a broader problem. Let me make this clear. We recognize that any health plan may accomplish some good, but at the same time by objectional features may not give return for the money expended, or may disturb certain relationships which should be retained if the plan is to meet with success.
For the safety of the state we have made commitments of $5 billion for defence. We require large sums for social security measures already in effect. Any political party which recommends the inauguration of a health plan must display a sense of
The Address-Mr. Blair responsibility and should not attempt to obtain political support by deliberately overlooking the difficulties in the way.
Let me emphasize that we stand for the introduction of a contributory health plan. When we form a government we will proceed with contributory national health insurance. But we think it should be carefully planned.
In the event of total war, there would be added a tremendous burden of taxes in addition to our already heavy commitments. The safety of Canada must rank first in our expenditures. In the process of development of a young nation there will be other expenditures of a nature vital to our growth and expansion. But we must realize also that medical science has infinitely more to give than the people receive. Professor Sigerist of the Johns Hopkins university has stated:
We could eliminate venereal diseases in a couple of years at the cost of one or two battleships, but we are not doing so.
We have solved more difficult economic problems in the past. When we are attacked by an enemy we can raise the money we need. Disease is also an enemy. It may have a less spectacular attack, but it is just as pernicious as actual warfare. We can find the funds to fight to a victorious end this war against disease and misery.
In view of the fact that the high cost of sickness and hospitalization is becoming beyond the financial means of our people, for the safety and benefit of the state we must eliminate deficiencies in our present health situation and lay the groundwork for a plan of national health. There has been too much glib talk about such a plan without getting down to certain basic and essential considerations. We hear statements from time to time that the reason health insurance is not introduced in Canada is that there are insufficient beds to carry out such a plan. When such a statement has been made there should also be added another potent reason- that health is under the jurisdiction of the provincial governments.
The following steps are necessary before any plan can be brought into effect. Any political statement that does not take these steps into consideration is futile.
1.	Under the British North America Act, except for marine and military services, health is under the control of the provinces. There must be no interference with that right.
2.	Before any plan can be brought into effect there must be further consultations with and between the dominion and the provinces, and agreement reached. It will be necessary to make financial agreements and allocation of funds.

The Address-Mr. Blair
3.	There must be a thorough investigation in advance as regards the best type of plan.
4.	The plan must meet the approval of municipal and provincial authorities. Medical authorities must be fully consulted, as to a large degree success of the plan rests with their approval.
We should proceed to lay the groundwork of the plan by calling a dominion-provincial conference and open discussions. I believe that all provinces are willing and anxious to better health conditions in their respective provinces, provided there is no interference with their rights to control health services. There should be a thorough investigation of conditions in addition to the mass of information already accumulated.
Because of the fact that municipalities are today so gravely concerned about their increasing obligations in connection with the construction of new hospital accommodation, and also the maintenance of existing hospitals, I have stated that the municipalities should have a part in any discussions that take place. Municipalities gain their power and existence through provincial legislation. The municipalities are the authorities mostly concerned with the responsibility of assuring that the hospitals continue to operate on a satisfactory scale. For this reason I would strongly emphasize their place in any preliminary discussions and in the steps which will lead up to satisfactory agreements.
As for the type of plan, let me state that some of the prepaid plans already in existence are unsatisfactory. Other plans are rendering excellent service. Very often people do not read the clauses in their contract, sometimes in small print, and find themselves where they are not fully covered for insurance. The hon. leader of the C.C.F. party (Mr. Coldwell) stated in his speech that the plan already in existence in England would be satisfactory.

Mr. Speaker, I want to take advantage of this opportunity to take part in this debate as there are one or two things I should like to draw to the attention of the government. Before I do that may I say that I support the amendment to the amendment moved by the leader of the C.C.F. (Mr. Coldwell). As the subamendment has been read two or three times I shall not read it again.
I think it is safe to say that national health insurance is long overdue. It was in the platform of the Liberal party in 1919 and has been discussed many times since. The government and other organizations have compiled about 40 reports in the last 30 years dealing with national health plans.
National health insurance is not something new. As a matter of fact many countries have had national health plans for a great many years. These countries are Norway, Sweden, Belgium, Denmark, New Zealand and the United Kingdom. Of the larger countries only three are without health insurance, namely, Canada, the United States and Australia; but Australia has a hospitalization plan of some kind. I had the privilege of meeting a group of parliamentarians from all over the commonwealth, and while we discussed many subjects naturally health insurance in the United Kingdom was one of the things we discussed. I talked with different members about the plan they have. There was general agreement that, while there might have been some difficulties in the plan when it was first introduced, it was today not only the most popular piece of legislation in the United Kingdom but also the most beneficial.
When we think of the various organizations that over the last several years have asked for a national health scheme or plan for this country, we find that they make a very impressive list. We have several representative organizations such as the federation of agriculture and other farm organizations, both national labour congresses-the American Federation of Labor and the Canadian Congress of Labour-the Canadian and Catholic Confederation of Labour, the railway transportation brotherhoods, the Canadian Legion, the board of evangelism of the United Church of Canada and numerous other organizations which have all asked for a national health plan.
It seems to me that if other countries can provide their people with health insurance there is no reason why Canada should lag behind. Travelling throughout the country one

meets very few people who have anything against health insurance. One runs up against the problem sometimes of where the money is going to come from. When we consider the cost of a national health plan we should remember that it will not be a new expense for the nation. We are already spending vast sums on health services which are inadequate. It is estimated that Canadians spent $500 million for medical and hospital bills last year, and our government spent $175 million for various health services. Altogether therefore the Canadian people, as individuals and as governments, spent approximately $675 million. That is something that people should remember, especially those who criticize health insurance on the ground that it would cost too much.
Health insurance would replace the amounts spent by individuals and would replace a large portion of the present expenditures by federal and provincial governments. The C.C.F. believes that the bulk of the cost can likely be met out of present budget surpluses and that there need not be any substantial increase in taxes to pay for it. However, if it is found necessary to make special financial provision to meet some of the cost the C.C.F. believes that the supplementary amount should be raised by a social security contribution graduated according to ability to pay.

I want to call attention to a matter that I raised last year. I spoke about the sewage disposal system at Roblin Park subdivision in my constituency. The department was good enough to make an investigation, but the engineer who was employed to make the investigation was the engineer who laid out the scheme in the first place. Surely the V.L.A. did not expect Mr. Scott, the engineer, to condemn his own work. If I hired someone to build a house and the occupants were not satisfied with the work done, it would be of no value to ask the man who built the house in the first place if he had done a good job. I am sure the same thing would be true in this case. Mr. Scott did the work in the first place, and having inspected the work is satisfied. In section 18 of his report he says:
With intelligent operation and maintenance therefor, I am of the opinion that these sewage disposal systems will give satisfactory service-as they did during the first years of operation. They need first however to be cleaned and freed of obstructions. Many an owner with a pump (a necessity) and hose and a few tools could do most of this work himself.
It is difficult to understand, after reading Mr. Scott's report, how he determines that this sewage system is in good shape, in view of the quality of the gravel and the distribution of the fluid throughout the field. Some digging was done and an examination of the laterals was conducted, but that was all that was done at Roblin Park. I understand that at some of the other places they did more.
In paragraph 4 Mr. Scott states that some of these tanks have given trouble-free service for from two to five years. About twenty disposal fields were frozen during the winter of 1946-47, which was the first year of operation. The number of frozen systems has steadily increased every year.
In paragraph 13, Mr. Scott states that his inspection revealed that in practically every


case the drainage tile was partly filled, and in some case completely plugged, with material which seemed to be tea leaves, coffee grounds and other such materials which did not disintegrate. Such materials should be classed as garbage and burned. At the time of the inspection the veterans requested the V.L.A. officials to have laboratory tests made to ascertain what really was in the pipes. I can find some of these veterans who would swear on a stack of bibles that they never put tea leaves or coffee grounds in that system.
I have some photographs here that I wanted to show the minister, but evidently he has stepped out of the house. When they dug up some of these fields they found that in some places the pipe was crushed by a stone. When the pipe is crushed flat it could not possibly allow the sewage through. In one case a hole was dug at the end of the lateral and then one of these roto-rooters was used. It was discovered that one pipe was about four inches below the other pipe. How could you expect such a system to work. This just shows the folly of sending a man who did the work in the first place to see if it works all right. If the department wants to do the fair thing for the veterans, they will send somebody else to look into it.
The following is a description of what was found at one residence:
Residence of H. A. Putman, 277 Pepperloaf Crescent- (1) Second lateral on the south side, removed piece of broken tile and after roto-rooter passed through and completely cleared the lateral. Level of this lateral too high to allow water to show at end when tank flushes.
(2) Third lateral on the south side cleared by roto-rooter. Also too high of level to show any water when tank flushes.
If I might explain, I would say that the tile is laid in a trench. The end of the trench next to the house is lower, so the water remains there and freezes. In another case the tile was laid in soft soil instead of hard-packed soil so that it would hold its position. The fill used was unsatisfactory because sand and large stones were used instead of the crushed stone. In some cases a test was made by plugging one end of the tile, and then when the tank was flushed no water appeared. This shows that the tile is not properly set. No purpose is served by going over all these cases, because they show the same thing. I was delighted when the minister said he would investigate the matter. I thought I had done something for the veterans. The investigation consisted of digging a hole, but the veterans are still pumping sewage out in that district.
Someone said the minister just came in, but I do not see him. I hope he will come in because I should like to talk to him about this matter. I do not know how long these

conditions are going to continue. I do not know how long the provincial sanitary-authorities are going to tolerate this condition in a district in which children are playing. I visited these homes before I left and found the men pumping out sewage. You may ask where they pump it. They pump it on to the next fellow's land and then he pumps it on to the next fellow's. The area used to be an old hay swamp, and the land is water-soaked. The soil will not absorb the sewage. I appeal to the minister to do something about this problem to assure the veterans a square deal. Things cannot go on as they are at the present time at Roblin Park. They need immediate attention. I have obtained these photographs to prove that what I am saying is correct. It is not something that somebody else told me and about which I am exaggerating. I was there. I saw the situation for myself. The actual photographs that were taken are here. A new school was built there, but those who built it certainly made sure that they did not run the sewer into the hay swamp this time. They ran it into the river, and I think that is the solution to this problem. There should be a large sewer system and it should be sent into the river. Nothing was good enough for these follows when they went to fight for us. Now that we have sold them houses, if the sewer system does not work their houses are worth about $1,000 less than they agreed to pay for them.
I want to say something about pork and the reduction in the floor price from 26 to 23 cents per pound which takes place on December 31. That is $4.50 a hog less that the farmer is going to take on January 1 than he will get on December 31. This reduction will certainly hit the small producer. A great many pigs are produced by the small men. It is a sideline with them, and this reduction in the floor price is going to hit them hard.
Another point to consider is that this price cut may actually force many pork producers out of the business altogether. This would result in a shortage, with pork becoming scarce and prices rising again. Is this not contrary to the policy of price stabilization, without which this industry is doomed to failure? Unless parity prices can be guaranteed over a reasonable period of time, enabling the producer to plan his industry, the inevitable result is instability. An inadequate floor price of 23 cents a pound, with no long-term markets assured, is bound to produce instability.
The government refers to this 23 cents as a floor price; but experience in the past has shown that government floor prices often become ceiling prices in actual practice.
The Address-Mr. Bryce Indeed, recent experience shows that there is no guarantee that the farm producers will receive even an inadequate floor price set by the government.
All these uncertainties come at a time when it is forecast-and I quote the economic division of the Department of Agriculture- that the net farm income will drop 5 per cent below that of a year ago; for farm operating costs and depreciation charges are higher than they were a year ago. The shortsightedness of the government's policy is illustrated by the fact that it is reducing the floor price two months before the United States embargo on Canadian meats is removed. It was announced by the minister that it will be removed on March 1, 1953. Why does the government not wait to determine what marketing conditions will exist in the United States after March 1? There is no assurance yet that our meat exports to the United States, when resumed, will be under the same conditions that prevailed prior to February 23 last. Indeed there are indications that the shortage of United States supplies which existed at this time last year- and upon which our meat exports depended- may have been substantially made up in the interim by the recent increase in production in that country. One does not have to be a prophet to foresee that once the United States is able to produce to meet its own needs, Canadian meat producers will again experience a loss of markets in that country.
There is also little prospect that the present commonwealth conference, even if it should prove to be a success, will be able to solve overnight the problems that hinder our trade with the United Kingdom. In this connection I wish to emphasize that it is my opinion that our government should take whatever steps are necessary to promote the maximum amount of trade at the earliest possible moment between Canada and the United Kingdom and other sterling countries. Instead of cutting production we should try to get some agreement with the United Kingdom. Get a five-year agreement and set a price. Then producers will know where they are as to price and the outlet for their produce.
Already there are plenty of signs that unless new market outlets for pork are forthcoming in the near future, serious curtailment of pork production will result. In some areas there has been an actual reduction of 30 per cent in sow breedings. I have here a clipping from the Rural Co-operator of November 27, 1952. The heading of the article is "Urges Hog Producers Avoid 'Same Old Stew' " and it reads as follows:
Bruce county survey of hog production from Tara to Port Elgin, and another survey in Carrick have

The Address-Mr. Crestohl shown a decline of about 30 per cent in sow breedings. These surveys will be taken every six months to direct the production of hogs.
The present drop indicates that if farmers keep the present number of sows they will be able to meet the limited market situation, but if any further breedings occur they will be in the same old stew with too many hogs.
Anybody wishing to take advantage of the 30 per cent decline in production, by breeding a large number of sows, is a short-sighted producer and has more concern for his own interests than the over-all good of the industry.

Why feed three sows when you can get just as much money by feeding two? Co-operation is necessary from every producer in trying to gauge our production to meet the market outlets.
The Federation of Agriculture will keep the farmer posted on production survey every six months. If as a result of this, speculators sneak into the business, it will mean that the steady producers will be asking for a controlled production.
The prospects for this important Canadian industry are not bright unless long-term markets with guaranteed stable prices can be obtained. I believe in forward prices. I have seen them in operation in New Zealand, Australia and Great Britain, and the farmers seem to favour them. If we would only try them on some things I think we would see how well they would go here.
I do not wonder why labour is always asking for an advance in wages. If we could stabilize farm prices and guarantee the farmer the same price for flv.e years, with certain qualifications, labour would then have no justification for asking for increased wages. Labour generally asks for increased wages when something has become scarce, when the farmer has not produced enough of it. Then they want higher wages to buy the product at the new prices. Therefore I think forward prices would do a wonderful job for the farmers, and at the same time they would stabilize prices in the whole country.

Mr. Speaker, first of all I wish to congratulate our two new colleagues on their excellent speeches in connection with the address in reply to the speech from the throne. The hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Deslieres) and the hon. member for Waterloo North (Mr. Schneider) have well maintained the dignity and good reputation of this house. I wish them a very successful parliamentary career. (Text):
I am moved to enter this debate by the glaring and inconceivable contradictions in the facts and the figures presented by hon. members on the opposite side of the house during the sessions of the present parliament. Their doing so can perhaps be epitomized in


the simple statement, that constant demands for large expenditures are made by them on one day, and equally vehement requests for reductions in taxes are made by them the next day. This, Mr. Speaker, is an obvious inconsistency. One cannot, even though he may be possessed of the most ingenious devices, call for increased expenditures and reduced taxes at the same time, and expect to achieve both objectives.
Let us first take a brief look at some of the additional expenditures and payments of large sums of money which have been and are constantly being urged by the hon. members of the opposition. They suggest, for example, that the government spend money for projects they consider so very vital to the interests of the country, such as the setting up of a national peace park-an item of extreme importance-without which our country could not progress. They further suggest that the government spend money to build a wall to protect an island near Toronto from erosion-another very vital matter that calls for expenditures, according to their judgment. They suggest that the government spend large sums of money to build an Alaska railway; to set up a modern merchant marine; to establish a bigger travel bureau and, Mr. Speaker, to give Great Britain a gift of $100 million and an additional credit of $80 million; also that we organize and set up a Pacific peace pact. These are suggestions that have come from the hon. members on the opposite side of the house. All of these they have suggested of their own motion, and in their burst of generosity they urge the government to supplement expenditures which already have been initiated by legislation of this house. They advise the government to increase the subsidies to farmers; to vote huge subsidies for federal aid to education and increase the subsidies to universities. They urge an increase in soldiers' pensions; an increase in old age pensions, and to make greater defence expenditures. Most recent of all, Mr. Speaker, they now urge the government to set up a national health plan.
I wish, Mr. Speaker, and I am certain the government does, too, that there was available sufficient money to do all these things without calling on the taxpayer for the necessary funds. But unfortunately there is no other way of doing so. To provide these funds would require a substantial increase in our national revenue and the consequent imposition of additional taxes. That is very obvious, but the irony of the situation is that with the request for all these things there is an overtone in what the hon. member for St. James (Mr. Beaudry) yesterday called a symphony,

calling for reduced taxes. That is just not possible, and I believe, Mr. Speaker, that the conductor of this inharmonious symphony knows full well that this music is nothing but an election air.
Why then are the house and the country consistently dunned by the continuous banging upon the bass drum for reduction of taxes? Of course the position taken by the opposition is obviously motivated by a desire to embarrass the government in power rather than to help the people. The Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) so very appropriately described these tactics in his address to the house on February 12 of last year, when he highlighted for an opposition the typical Tammany Hall precept: Never vote for a tax measure, and never oppose a public expenditure. It is therefore very simple to detect that this constant paradoxical and contradictory position has ominous motives. Is it the welfare of the country that is considered first, or is it the welfare of a political party that is sought?
Political parties must essentially place the interests of the country before the interests of their party. A famous British statesman once said: "My God comes first; my king comes next; my country follows, and then, and only then, my party". It is my respectful submission, Mr. Speaker, that the tactics of the hon. gentlemen of the opposition ignore this dictum and disclose a lamentable preference for party interest over the welfare of the country as a whole. That is sad indeed.
Why do they choose to forget the great advances made by our country in every way, and choose instead unjustifiably to harp on trivial, relatively unimportant matters? These manoeuvres, Mr. Speaker, are intended only to befog and obscure the progress of our country, and because of this it is necessary to remind the people again and again of the great achievements that have been attained.
Let the people of Canada judge from the record-from the whole record, Mr. Speaker, and not from incomplete extracts slanted for political purposes. And in looking at the record, Mr. Speaker, I am not so much concerned with the fortuitous and accidental discoveries and the worth of our natural resources; but I do want to look at the record showing the direct results of the planning, ingenuity, foresight, courage and daring of men, men of government, who I admit may not be faultless, but who nevertheless have proven by their accomplishments a perspicacity and judgment which merits the fullest and fairest recognition by all men of justice, irrespective of what side of the house they may sit on.
The Address-Mr. Crestohl
Referring, for example, to our advances in direct and intimate welfare and benefits to the people of our country, I cite only some of the legislation which our government has enacted: The veterans' charter which, together with subsequent amendments, provides for our heroes and their dependents in a way which is a model, excels similar legislation in any other country in the world. Is this a cause for criticism and for impeding the government's progress? Our legislation on unemployment insurance, family allowances and old age security is such that it challenges similar legislation in any other country, and provides our people with a social welfare program as good as if not better than any in the world. And no other country, Mr. Speaker, within such a short space of time provided its people with better social security legislation. It may hurt politically for our friends to admit this, but as men of honour and truth they cannot help but agree, and admire it. Is this a reason why our government should be criticized, ridiculed and sniped at from every salient?
Now let us have a further look at the record from the international standpoint. Our country, in proportion to its means and population, during the last seven years has done more for the preservation of peace throughout the world than any other country. This is a universally accepted fact. The dedication of our diplomats stands out over that of the diplomats of the entire world in this phase of international relations to the point where the recognition of the world acclaims the wisdom and the sense of justice of our representatives by offering to them the most responsible posts in international councils.
Is this cause for justifiable criticism? Again I emphasize that, as hon. gentlemen, our friends on the opposite side must admit -perhaps with a secret and glowing pride- the soundness of these facts.
All records disclose that our commercial and industrial progress has been truly miraculous and amazing. I use the term miraculous because our Minister of Trade and. Commerce (Mr. Howe) accomplished what he did notwithstanding the prophets of doom, some of whom sit on the opposition benches and who predicted insurmountable depression, unemployment, hunger, the collapse of our economy, the halting of industry and the impossibility of doing anything advantageous for the people of Canada. But let us see briefly what world opinion thinks of our position today. In this connection I

The Address-Mr. Crestohl quote an extract from Time magazine of February 4, 1952 where, at page 25, it states:
Since 1939, Canada has: Quadrupled her national production, made a 50 per cent advance in the Canadian standard of living, raising her average income for a family of four to $4,000 a year-$622 above the corresponding U.S. average, kept her finances in splendid solvency.
Canada's growing industrial muscle has expanded her world influence to an extent never before achieved by a country of 14 million inhabitants. The swelling flood of foodstuffs, metals, oil, newsprint and goods flowing from her fields, forests, mines and factories has given Canada a position of importance in the free world's councils subordinate only to the U.S. and Britain. Canada now supplies:
More than 90 per cent of the free world's nickel, and an important share of the zinc, copper, aluminum, and other strategic metals for the west's defence.
Half the world's newsprint; three out of five of the world's newspaper pages are printed on Canada paper.
A growing share of North America's oil and natural gas from the new-found Alberta fields, the "Texas of the north".
A substantial supply of uranium for U.S. atomic bombs.
The world's second-biggest export wheat crop, a source of food for 71 nations.
Canada's vast area throbs with industrial action.
This spirit of growing confidence, both at home and abroad, has helped attract an ample supply of fresh capital to keep the boom going. Canadian investors, who were once somewhat timid about their own prospects, last year plowed back a record 22 per cent of their national income into new development. United States, British and Swiss capital is rushing into the bullish Canadian market. American investors have put more than $7 billion into Canada, the heaviest U.S. stake in any foreign country. And the flow is increasing steadily, as Canada shows that she has both the wealth and the men to work it.
The free nations overseas also look to thriving Canada for assistance. She is the only member besides the U.S. who can pay her own way and help the other eleven countries of the North Atlantic alliance. Canada has already shipped $145-4 million worth of arms to NATO allies and has sent troops to Korea and Europe. But more is expected, and from a nation of Canada's strength and promise, more will surely come.
I should like to add that similar opinions in various forms have been expressed repeatedly in leading financial, commercial and industrial publications in most of the democratic countries of the world. That is what the world thinks of the achievements of our government, and the present position of our country. Well, the right hon. minister has performed the impossible. I am reminded of a quip which was produced in a reply by an Israeli when he was questioned, in wondrous amazement, about the things being done by his little country which appeared impossible. He was asked, "How do you manage to do all these things? Some of them are impossible; the other things are extremely difficult." "Ah", replied the Israeli, "we have a system. First of all we do the impossible things, and then when we have a little more


time we do the difficult ones." That, perhaps, is the secret weapon of our efficient minister. First of all he does the things that seem impossible, the things that hon. members on the other side of the house thought were impossible, and when he has a little spare time he does the difficult things.
There is the record on this level. Can these accomplishments and achievements be criticized justifiably? Is this not a truly miraculous record of progress? Should this not provoke the admiration of hon. members of the opposition, if they considered the welfare of the country before the welfare of their party? What, then, is the resultant status of these prophets of doom when, in the face of their predictions, just the reverse has been achieved? Some hon. members opposite saw discouragement, depression, want, hunger and an ominous future for our country. On this side of the house men looked upward with courage, determination and conviction and, in spite of continuous road-blocks, this record of achievement which I have just presented was attained.
We then come to the great concern of hon. members of the opposition with respect to the reduction of taxes. If the opposition was sincerely anxious to keep taxes down, why did it not oppose the financial assistance voted to the victims of the Fraser river floods, to the extent of $5 million for rehabilitation and $4,500,000 for repairing and strengthening dikes? They did not oppose it because it was not politically wise for them to do so. Why did they not oppose the voting of funds to assist the victims of the Rimouski fire, to the extent of $2,500,000? Oh no, it was not wise for them to oppose it. And the same thing applies to the victims of the Cabano fire, to the extent of $300,000. Why did they not oppose and vote against the contributions to the victims of the Red river flood, to the extent of an interim payment of $12,500,000 plus 75 per cent of all re-diking costs? Why did they not vote against the grants to universities in the sum of $7 million? Why did they not vote against the bill to establish old age pensions to the extent of an estimated $365 million a year or $1 million per day for every day of the year? Why did they not oppose and vote against the payment of family allowances to the extent of an estimated $350 million?
At the time these requests came before the house, not only did members of the opposition fail to oppose these expenditures; on the contrary they approved them unanimously because it was then politically wise for them to do so. But what do they do today? Today when political exigency makes it advisable they change their tune and

accuse the government of overspending, which makes taxes high. If they had voted against these measures I could understand their statements today about high taxes, but having voted for these expenditures they know full well, and the country does too, that their complaint is nothing but a purely political outcry.
These tactics are so obvious that they require no emphasis. So are the tactics disclosed by the following specious type of criticism which we have been hearing. If ministers travel in their line of duty the opposition refer to them as flitting about the country for political purposes. If they do not travel and remain in Ottawa at their desks, they are criticized for being arm chair diplomats. If they are on the alert for preparedness against a sudden attack and stockpile essential supplies, they are criticized for overspending. If they do not take the necessary precautions they are criticized for exposing the security of the country to grave danger. If they vote allowances to veterans they are criticized for creating a need for higher taxation. If they do not, they are criticized for neglecting the heroes of our country. If the government subsidizes education in Canada there is another outcry of throwing a burden on the taxpayer. If they do not, they are charged with neglecting the future citizens of the country. If the government makes provision for needy families, indigents and the older citizens of our country, they are criticized again for making it necessary to impose taxes. If they do not, they are criticized for being indifferent to the progress of social security measures. If taxes are not reduced, the government is most severely criticized. If taxes are reduced, the government is accused of doing it for political purposes.
