Exactly; hear, hear. How far can a political party go with this double talk? Do hon. members of the opposition really think they can hoodwink an intelligent public by singing one tune one day and another tune the next day? It is apparent that the hon. gentlemen are attempting to focus the attention of the Canadian public on unimportant trivialities in order to detract their attention from the basic and important things achieved by the government of this country.
I was astounded to hear intelligent men make an issue of 14,000 serving forks, or even three times 14,000. If sufficient serving forks were not available then the very same gentlemen would complain from the floor of this house that our men were being neglected and deprived of the most primitive comforts.
68108-25i
The Address-Mr. Crestohl I was equally surprised to listen to a complaint that essential stores and supplies are stockpiled for the armed forces; too many shoes, too many uniforms, too many raincoats. What a cry would come from the floor of this house if a shooting war was to break out and the country was not prepared to provide uniforms, clothing and shoes for the many thousands of men and women who would suddenly be projected into military service.
Is that not the better part of wisdom rather than to be caught short? Ah, but it makes good ground for criticism, and so it is exploited to the limit. I am confident that the Canadian people will see through these beguiling tactics.
How amusing too is the issue made about neckties. So the army has ordered three times the number of neckties that there are men in the services. I do not know how often the army issues neckties, but I know they certainly wear out very quickly. But even this is used as a basis for criticism, insignificant as the item is. I am certain that this argument only helps to emphasize to the people of Canada how very shallow and puerile are the grounds for the criticism levelled by the opposition against the government.
At this point I should like to commend the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) for the full and satisfactory explanation he gave the house with respect to the forks, neckties, shoes, uniforms and raincoats. He most thoroughly exploded the entire myth which the hon. gentlemen opposite have attempted to create, a myth which was without any substance and was even devoid of sound political air to the opposition. I feel certain that he left nothing unexplained which could be the basis for criticism in any of these trivial matters. In fact I consider it a high compliment which the opposition is paying quite unwittingly to the government when for its criticism it has nothing more serious with which to make an assault than these insignificant matters. After all, when you reflect upon the tremendous obligations which the government is called upon to discharge and the fantastic responsibilities which the government carries and you find nothing more serious to criticize, then I say that even if they are true-and indeed they are not-the over-all consequence of this great but empty demonstration by the opposition is a mark of the greatest flattery to the government.
I am sure that the people of Canada understand this and they no doubt realize by reaction that this country has had, indeed, a fine, trustworthy and competent government.

The Address-Mr. Crestohl The many facets of its responsibilities are almost faultlessly co-ordinated by a competent administration which has placed our country in the enviable position in which it is. What more could have been done?
Canada has acquired a position of preeminence throughout the world. How much greater could such an achievement be? How much more recognition could our diplomats bring to Canada than to be amongst the topmost diplomats in the world? Our currency is the strongest in the world. If we take a look at Canada today, impartially and purely objectively, we will see a country which abundantly discloses a steadily expanding prosperity in every field of trade, commerce and industry. We will see a country with a minimum of unemployment or poverty, a country whose people earn reasonably satisfactory salaries for their labours. We will see a country in which there is an abundance of food and comforts, a country with an enviable educational system available to every child. We will see a country which enjoys most respectful international relations. We will see a country with the finest social security program in the world, a country in which there is full and complete enjoyment by everyone of the four basic freedoms-yes, Mr. Speaker, a country which is a model of true democracy.
What more, therefore, could any country in the world wish for? We are indeed blessed. Let us all recognize it, every one of us, government, opposition,. the people of Canada, and let us work together to preserve it, not to change it, but to preserve it, in peace and national unity, for our ever-growing country and for the generations that will follow.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, being a new member it is with hesitation that I venture to take part in this debate. I desire first to join other hon. members in extending my compliments and congratulations to the mover (Mr. Deslieres) and the seconder (Mr. Schneider) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne for the excellent manner in which they acquitted themselves in their first addresses to hon. members of this house. I certainly go along with the hon. member for Waterloo North in extending my compliments to the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi for his fluency in both French and English. It is an attainment which I should like to achieve even if in a much lesser degree. Having entered parliament on the same day as these two hon. members, I feel a friendly and neighbourly kinship toward them even though they appear to have been misled in their early political training. Nevertheless I am very glad to compliment them as I feel they made a good contribution to the debate and performed a service for their constituencies.
Just as the hon. member for Waterloo North spoke with pride of the industry, thrift, integrity and other qualities of the people of his constituency, I can likewise claim those qualities for the people of my constituency. Yes, I can claim them for both French and English. We live and work side by side and enjoy the best of relations. Like people in other parts of the maritimes we respect ourselves, we respect each other and share a common pride in our community life, in the industries and institutions which have been built up in the lands by the sea.
I should like at this time to pay a compliment to my predecessor, a man beloved by the people of my constituency to whom he gave unstinting service until his passing. Although in poor health during the last year he never spared himself and always put the interests of his people first. The loyal friendship of one's associates is an outstanding achievement, and that the late Mr. H. H. Hatfield attained.
I should also like to congratulate at this time the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair) and the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Campney) on their promotion to the cabinet. The hon. member for Coast-Capilano of course is no stranger to us in New Brunswick. He has been down there before, but now that he has become

Minister of Fisheries I am sure we will welcome him a great deal more because in the maritimes we are very much interested in his department.
Since becoming a member of this house I have listened with a great deal of interest to the speeches of hon. members. One cannot help but be conscious of the privilege and responsibility of helping to shape and build this vast country of ours which we are so proud to call Canada. The House of Commons is the nerve centre of our nation where east meets west and the central section is the host. The problems, privileges and obligations of the two great races in this vast area are discussed as well as the requirements of different sections of our country, and by a tolerant democratic method we hammer out on the anvil of good will laws that serve to unify this great land.
One cannot help but be inspired by the surroundings of parliament hill. On every hand you see evidence of statesmen who have, each in his own way, contributed to the building of Canada as a great democracy, a country which today in a very troubled world is an outstanding example of unity, tolerance and prosperity of people of different races, languages and habits.
This takes me back to my own constituency, a lovely section of New Brunswick lying in the beautiful Saint John river valley, settled and hewed from the wilderness by French and English speaking people who have continued to live in harmony side by side during the last 125 years. It is a portion of my province which we hope in the near future will become industrialized in large measure as a result of hydro development which at the present time is under study.
When I speak of "capital" you may think of property, stocks and bonds; but to the people of my province, and I think to the people of the maritimes generally, the word has another meaning. It is the capital of the spirit which is not only the basis of our economy but is our very way of life.
The people of my riding depend upon mixed farming, lumber and potatoes. As many hon. members know, potatoes have become a highly specialized crop with a great potential value on the one hand but a tremendous risk on the other. Potato raisers may become wealthy in a few years but just as quickly may face bankruptcy. There is something very fascinating about handling and raising potatoes. Large fields of potatoes in blossom are a beautiful picture, and when I refer to large fields I refer to hundreds of acres in some places.
This year the potato grower is very happy. His "spuds", as we call them, are a reasonably good price and are likely to remain
The Address-Mr. Montgomery so until the crop is cleaned up. However, it is a crop that cannot be carried over. The amount of money a potato farmer ties up annually in seed, fertilizer, spray materials, help and machinery is tremendous, to say nothing of his investment in land and necessary storage facilities. That is why in years of no market or low prices bankruptcy stares these men in the face and, make no mistake about it, the year 1950-51 put a lot of farmers on the rocks. They fell back on grain, hay and stock, but due to the drought this year hundreds of acres of the oat crop were not even harvested. In my constituency a good part of the grain crop that was harvested has not given more than a 50 per cent return. This season has created a difficult situation for the mixed farmer. He has no grain to sell, but still worse he is faced with the prospect of having to buy feed or dispose of his stock. Either of these possibilities would be disastrous and, notwithstanding the hardship of the coming winter, they will face another seeding season empty-handed. A situation such as we are facing this season in my constituency is discouraging, to say the least. Those who were able to finance a potato crop last spring are having a feast, while the mixed farmer is facing a famine.
Our farmers have no market for hay, and no substantial market for beef or pork. However, the farmers are hopeful now that the United States government has announced its intention of lifting the embargo in the near future. This may afford an outlet for our hay, but the farmers have been reducing their hog production.
The farmers inform me that when the English market was lost, there was no other to take its place. It is for this reason that the farmers in my province are hoping something good will come out of the commonwealth prime ministers' conference now being held in London which the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) are attending. The people will follow the proceedings closely, because they want to see the United Kingdom markets reopened to Canadian farm products. The leading daily newspaper in New Brunswick, the Telegraph-Journal, after mentioning in its issue of November 26 that the Prime Minister had left for London, stated:
The meeting he will attend, the commonwealth prime ministers' conference opening in London on Thursday (the 27th), will be the biggest thing of its kind since the Ottawa conference of 1932.
We in the maritimes must have outside markets, markets that can be relied upon year after year. The farmers in my part of the province will tell you-in fact they have told me-that the United States market is not reliable. If the United States is short of
390	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Montgomery a commodity it is easy to enter their market, but ordinarily they are our greatest competitor in world markets for agricultural commodities. While they may be friendly rivals, they are nevertheless ruthless and businesslike in all their dealings. I am informed that the farm lobby in Washington is one of the most potent political forces in United States politics, ever on the alert to. see that Canadian producers get a minimum of access to the United States food market. For these reasons and others, no long-term scheme for absorbing Canadian surplus production can be arranged with the United States.
I should like to remind hon. members of this house that when our farmers are unfortunate enough to lose their grain crops because of drought, as many in my riding lost their grain crop this year, there is no relief such as the western farmer may receive under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. I understand, of course, that the western farmers make a contribution under that act. It was for this reason, Mr. Speaker, that in my opening remarks I referred to "the capital of the spirit". The farmers of my province have to meet the ups and downs of uncertain markets by ingenuity in finding ways and means of carrying on and providing such prosperity and security as may be obtained through hard work, long hours and strict economy.
It is understandable, therefore, why we in the provinces by the sea are vitally interested in markets for agricultural commodities. We realize that any agricultural policy for Canada must be elastic because of our vast area and the different conditions and requirements of each area. But I must say, Mr. Speaker, and I think I fairly represent the opinion of the farmers of my province, they feel it is the responsibility of the government to do everything possible in finding and developing export markets as well as assisting in the home market.
Agriculture, industry and trade are very much tied together in this world of varying monetary systems and different standards of living. While it is recognized that the hon. members responsible have no easy task, nevertheless, because it is a vital matter to our primary producers, I am sure that all hon. members are fervently hoping for some tangible agreement under which commonwealth trade will start to flow more freely. If such an agreement is made, perhaps some form of permanent trade arrangement may be made that will provide a reliable and profitable outlet for our farmers' products. We are hoping that these results will flow from the conference now taking place in


London, in which our own Prime Minister will no doubt play a prominent role.
Having listened with interest to the speeches thus far, I felt compelled to take part in this debate in order to bring to the hon. members of this house the views of many people in my constituency, and to place their problems and difficulties before you. I feel that the solution of many of the problems of my province lies in an agricultural policy of some permanence, so that our small, mixed farmers may proceed to develop their lands on a planned economy which will give them a feeling of security and contentedness.
In conclusion I should like to say a word or two concerning a national health scheme. There is nothing in the speech from the throne that would grant the ordinary citizen relief from taxation or give him some feeling of comfort and protection in matters of health. As the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Catherwood) so well stated, there is nothing in the speech from the throne that would indicate "relief and the end of the sacrifices of the past few years". Since there appears to be no hope that the ordinary fellow who lives around the corner or across the tracks will receive better treatment, I commend my leader for proposing the amendment to the speech from the throne, and I can wholeheartedly support it.
Let me repeat what I said a few minutes ago. We are here as representatives of all parts of Canada to make laws, but according to the tolerant democratic method. This is the highest level of government in our country, and is often referred to as the federal government. How did this federal government become a reality? How did our constitution in Canada come into being? Was it not by consultation and agreement? Did not the representatives of various sections of this country get together and work out an agreement on which the British North America Act was based?
That was over 80 years ago, and many things have changed in 80 years. There have been changes that have created many problems that were never dreamed of then. In the light of such changes, further consultation among the partners in confederation-the provinces and the federal government- should again take place, in an atmosphere of tolerance and give and take, in order to sincerely try to arrive at a solution that will benefit all the people at various levels of government.
I know there have been conferences, but rightly or wrongly the people of my province -and I believe the same is true in many other provinces-feel that the federal government

is not meeting the provinces half-way. They feel that the dominion government is taking the lion's share of the national revenue. I say this, Mr. Speaker, because I believe it expresses the feeling of the people. After all, Ottawa is a long way from the homes of most citizens of Canada but the municipal government is on their doorstep, even closer than the provincial government; it therefore can be more closely supervised and more easily understood.
All governments realize, or should, that there is a limit beyond which taxation should not go unless there is a national emergency. But a proper distribution of such revenues is the problem upon which there has not been agreement. As I see it, that is the reason for my leader's amendment. If it were not so, why would a group representing the mayors of cities in every part of Canada be appearing before this government? While this group represents only the cities, other municipalities have problems which are just as serious. Coming as I do from a small town, and having had considerable interest in rural municipalities, I know that the problems with regard to education, hospital and medical care or health services are tremendous. It is growing beyond the resident taxpayers' ability to provide these services, even with all the assistance that comes from provincial governments, part of which in turn comes from Ottawa.
Mr. Speaker, I am not going into all the reasons that have helped to create this heavy burden. Suffice it for me to say that it is a live issue. Many people cannot afford to have the necessaries of our standard of living, let alone to be sick. No one is ill by choice. Illness comes like a thief in the night. Sooner or later, on account of illness, anyone may be faced with obligations that he just cannot pay. It is no answer to tell these poor people: "Sorry; the municipality must look after you. It is their problem." As far as the legal responsibility is concerned, they know that they are part of the municipality. They also know that the municipality has not the wherewithal to help them.
I like the expression coined by my colleague the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr) when he said that our democracy should work like a family; that the federal government is considered the senior or daddy of the family, so the lesser lights look to daddy. Is there much wonder that they do so, in view of the tremendous sums of revenue collected by daddy? This is why the mayors of cities are waiting upon this government. Unless some logical rearrangement satisfactory to all governments is worked out, the delegations will not be confined to representatives
The Address-Mr. Studer of the cities. I am no alarmist. In my humble way I am trying to bring to the attention of the government some of the problems of the ordinary people who feel that they have been forgotten.
Before closing I think it fair that I should place myself on record in reference to the amendment to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Cold-well). As I understand the constitutional issue and set-up, it seems to me that the government is being asked to do something which it is not yet in a position to carry out, namely to bring down at this session legislation providing for a national health insurance program. I am not convinced that sufficient groundwork has been done and that a common formula has been worked out with the provinces. Hence I cannot see my way clear to support the amendment to the amendment. But that fact does not in the least indicate that I am opposed to a sound health scheme. On the contrary, I am fully in accord with a scheme worked out jointly between the dominion and the provincial governments as a national health program in order to bring to families in the low and the ordinary income brackets-yes, possibly to all-the assurance that they will receive the necessary medical and hospital care when required, without the worry and hardship entailed in having to pay the bill.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

This
evening, Mr. Speaker, the people whom I represent in the constituency of Maple Creek, in the southwest corner of the province of Saskatchewan, - would want to associate themselves with me in extending the good wishes and the congratulations of all of us to the mover (Mr. Deslieres) and the seconder (Mr. Schneider) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. They would also want me to say to those who may be fortunate enough to attend the coronation of Her Majesty the Queen in England next summer:	Give our good wishes to our
sovereign, that she may have the good fortune and the blessing of the Almighty upon

The Address-Mr. Studer her so that her reign may be long and glorious in the interests of all her subjects.
We represent our constituencies; therefore it is our duty to present the problems, if any, of these constituencies to the government and to the houses of parliament. In my endeavour to discharge that duty as it applies to me I would ask your indulgence for a few minutes to listen to the conditions that exist in that great constituency of Maple Creek. Conditions there today differ from those which existed at other times when I have had the privilege of speaking about that constituency. We have had a good crop this year in most of my constituency. In spite of the generally good crop conditions all over the west-which please everyone and add greatly to the wealth of Canada, since every bushel of wheat means approximately another $1.50 added to the general wealth of the people of all Canada, because we all derive benefit from it-in spite of that good fortune, nevertheless there are parts of the constituency of Maple Creek in which prairie farm assistance payments, that is crop failure payments, will again be made this year.
The reason for that is this. In that country the constituencies are large. A constituency is a whole country in itself, much larger than some of the provinces of Canada. The result is that a change in weather conditions can be very pronounced, and what may bring good conditions in one area can bring about most unfortunate conditions in another. But altogether, over the whole, we have been blessed with good fortune during the past year.
In addition to that, Maple Creek is the type of constituency, and its area is so vast, that if there are any abnormal conditions they are bound to exist there. In spite of the many times it has been my duty to point out that crop failures have existed due to drought in that constituency, this year we have had the very opposite. We have had flood conditions in that constituency, believe it or not. We had flood conditions that created for the individual just as great havoc as the flood condition at Winnipeg of a year or two ago. Although not on as extensive a scale, yet to the individual the loss was just as great. In the constituency of Maple Creek we have over 90 per cent of the irrigation in the province of Saskatchewan. We had flood conditions in that constituency which inundated whole towns such as Eastend. Towns were under water for a period of approximately a month. All the people had to be removed from those towns lying in those valleys because of the abnormal conditions.

The snow, which thawed too rapidly, produced a volume of water that no precautions could have prevented. It flooded irrigation projects, and the people living in the valleys of Eastend and Valmarie were flooded out. We almost had a tragic situation at Swift Current, Saskatchewan, where the Duncairn dam, through almost superhuman efforts of the P.F.R.A. officials, was prevented from collapsing and inundating a large part of that city.
Because of those conditions those people have suffered heavy losses. The P.F.R.A. officials went to extreme lengths to recondition the lands, rehabilitate the irrigation ditches, rebuild the streets of the towns, pump the water from the basements and make it possible for those people to go back to the towns and take up living where they left off. In the meantime many of the farmers lost their seed grain, lost their feed, lost some livestock, and had difficulty in re-establishing themselves. Some of the men on those lands are returned men.
I think under those conditions the province of Saskatchewan should have been much more willing to help out in the emergency. Officials of the province come to Ottawa and ask the federal government to assist in rehabilitating and financing the work that has to go on in those areas. As I see the situation, it was not a national disaster. As I pointed out, it was a disaster to the individual, but it was not a national disaster when compared with the Winnipeg floods and the fires in Rimouski and in other places.
Generally, the situation in connection with financing losses of that kind is this. If the loss is within the $100 class or category the municipality takes care of it. If it comes within the hundreds of thousands of dollars category, the provincial government takes care of it. If it comes within the category of millions of dollars, then the federal government takes care of it. Therefore I ask the province to reimburse those people who have suffered financial losses. If they cannot finance the situation, if the amount involved is too great, then they should come to the federal government and the federal government will consider whether or not the province can finance it. I have never known the federal government to take an attitude at any time that is not responsive to the demands of any province, any municipality or any people in difficulty. I ask the province to rehabilitate those people and place them in the financial position they deserve, as has been done when other people have found themselves in difficulty.

If any province or any area suffered from the affliction of foot-and-mouth disease, certainly the constituency of Maple Creek did, because it comprises much of the ranching area of southern Saskatchewan and of the whole of Saskatchewan. I do not know of any area that was more affected by anything that happened to the beef industry than we were when the foot-and-mouth disease disaster struck us. Another thing that afEects us is the distance from all the ports through which we ship our wheat. We are practically the same distance from Churchill as we are from Vancouver, and as we are from Fort William. That being the case, we in the southwest portion of the province are usually the last to be served in the delivery of our wheat because, as everyone knows, if there is a shortage of box cars or a shortage of space, or if deliveries of certain grades of grain have to be made on account of sales to other countries at the appropriate time, in order to make the sales those box cars can be utilized twice as often from practically any point in Manitoba to Fort William, as they could be from southwest Saskatchewan.
So just until recently we were practically still on the five-bushel quota. And while I am talking about that I hope the wheat board takes an interest in this matter, and that before all the other wheat delivery quotas are raised they will provide facilities for southwest Saskatchewan in order to equalize their quota deliveries with people in the other provinces.
Much has been mentioned about the farm storage proposition in western Canada. When there are heavy crops a great deal of farm storage becomes necessary, and the problem becomes acute. This is especially so when it is impossible to deliver your grain under the quota system. I do not know of any way to circumvent this except by providing more box cars. There is no way of limiting this except by providing more storage space.
It has been suggested by some that the government should provide facilities or make advances to the farmers so they could store farm grain. What I need in southwestern Saskatchewan is room enough for my grain so I will get the full value for it in relation to the money spent in its production, and so I do not have to borrow money and pay interest on it, and have to repay it at some future date. I have never had any trouble in borrowing money; my trouble has always been in repaying it. If facilities could be provided so there would be plenty of room for storage facilities on the farms or in the cities, through elevator storage facilities, and through government storage elevators that might pay for themselves in time-and they have paid for themselves and would pay for 68108-26
The Address-Mr. Studer themselves-then I think that southwest area of Saskatchewan, which certainly has been overlooked in connection with government terminal elevator storage and those specialized facilities, would be satisfied.
I think the government could very well consider those additional facilities either at Shaunavon or at Swift Current, and for a twofold purpose. They would be useful in conditions such as we have had in the last few years, and also when there are conditions of drought and large parts of the province are faced with crop failure. The result would be to keep the economy of that country in better condition, and there would be feed grain and seed grain in an area where it would be needed.
Only too often have the farmers in southwestern Saskatchewan had to pay freight for seed and feed from Fort William, or from some other parts of Saskatchewan and Manitoba, arising from crop failures which have [DOT] occurred through no fault of their own. I think proper storage facilities should be provided in southwestern Saskatchewan, and no one would lose any money on it.
There has been much talk in regard to loans to farmers on the grain. Last year in this house and again this year there has been discussion as to the amount of money that should be provided in loans or guarantees of loans to farmers who had their wheat in the snow last year and were unable to deliver this year. There was a whole lot of talk and a lot of difficulty in connection with providing a guarantee or a loan to the extent of $20 million to farmers last year. As a matter of interest, the amount actually used by farmers under that loan which was made available by the Prairie Grain Producers Interim Financing Act was $625,671.41, out of a total of $20 million.
I say again that the farmer wants a place to deliver his grain in southwestern Saskatchewan, and a place to store it as a secondary feature. We say the farmer in southwestern Saskatchewan does not want a system whereby he is going to be compelled to pay storage charges for other farmers throughout the length and breadth of the three western provinces, who can well afford to keep their grain. And if storage is paid on the grain, then the people in southwestern Saskatchewan who over a period of years have had about twelve bushels to the acre will be paying storage on the grain of other farmers in the three western provinces. Unless a new system can be devised, then the farmers in southwestern Saskatchewan will be penalized for charges that others are not obliged to pay.

We had an instance of it the other day when a comparison was made between the subsidy that was paid to the farmers or allowed to the farmers under the Agricultural Prices Support Act during the past year, amounting to $10 million, and the subsidy paid to the gold mining industry of $40 million-a most unfair comparison if I ever heard one, because there is no similarity between them.
The Agricultural Prices Support Act provided some $200 million to stabilize the market for farm products when the price was low. It was not established to lose money, but rather to stabilize the prices of the farmers' products for a period of time. If they were not stabilized, the farmer lost money.
If you wish to make a comparison of farming and the gold mining industry in the matter of subsidies, then make a comparison between the subsidy that has actually been paid the farmers, and that has nothing at all to do with the Agricultural Prices Support Act. I have here in the Western Producer of October 9, 1952-and no one can say that this is a Liberal paper-a record of the federal government's action in subsidizing agriculture. The actual amount paid in subsidies to the agricultural industry across Canada from 1940 to 1950-51 has been $853,300,000, or more than three-quarters of a billion dollars. That has been the subsidy paid to agriculture during that time.
Let us compare that with the subsidy paid to the gold mining industry, and we will have the answer. Do not let anyone get the idea that I think the gold mining industry in Canada is in trouble. I do not know, but it seems to me the people handling that can take care of themselves pretty well. Yet I know this, that there are almost a million people engaged in gold mining, or who are earning their living from that industry. I also know that the incentive offered by gold mining has spread to other valuable minerals being produced. The incentive offered by gold mining has induced the prospector to 

go out to find other valuable minerals throughout the country. This subsidy has encouraged the gold mining industry, so that we could make the most of our mineral resources.
Let my hon. friends in Saskatchewan who are complaining about the subsidy to gold mining remember that we have the largest uranium discovery in the world in northern Saskatchewan. I am not too much concerned about the gold mining industry; I am not worried about it. I have not been troubled at any time with having too much gold under my control, and I think the same thing can be said for most of the farmers in southwestern Saskatchewan. There has never been an overabundance of gold under their control. It is a lack of gold or its equivalent that has caused a difficult situation in south Saskatchewan and the difficulties that have been inflicted upon the farmers there during past years.
If it is possible to keep a million people employed in this country, I want to see those people employed. I want to see them have the right to earn a living whether at gold mining, in industry, in oil, in agriculture, in our manufacturing plants, on our railroads or wherever they may be. Those people have a right to live and it is the government's duty to provide a means whereby they can earn a living. That is a duty the government owes to all the inhabitants of the country. If the government finds it necessary to provide a gold subsidy to maintain this million people at work, what can I do but support it in the hope that the gold mining industry along with agriculture and all other industries will prosper so that subsidies will not be needed in the future.
Something has been said about the wheat situation. I think the position in this regard can be summarized in a very few words. This government has faced tremendous problems in the last few years. The wheat board and the Department of Trade and Commerce were faced with over a billion bushels of grain last year and with more than that this year, or over two billion bushels in twenty-four months. At least half that amount has been moved. Facilities have been provided and markets found under the most adverse conditions. Over 240 million bushels of damp and tough grain has been moved at a reasonable price. That is one of the greatest accomplishments ever achieved in Canada or any country in the world.
I do not say that is good enough. Nothing is good enough in the Liberal party. If there is anything bad, they are determined to make

it good. That is the Liberal policy. If it is good they are determined to make it better. If it is wrong, they will make it right. If it is right, they will bring it to perfection. That is what we subscribe to.
The international wheat agreement will shortly be coming up again for consideration. Let no one in Canada think for one moment that every effort is not going to be made to obtain the best possible results in connection with the wheat agreement for the benefit of the farmers of this country. We are not going to have a fire sale. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) will never agree to give our wheat away at any price nor attempt to blast our way into the markets of the world at any price. We are going to obtain for that wheat what it is worth, plus, in all the markets of the world; we will obtain what the markets of the world will be willing to pay. We are not going to price ourselves out of the markets of the world. There are two times when agriculture gets into difficulty; one is when there is no production, when there is a crop failure, and the other is when there is too much wheat. Our friends the socialists wish to give our production away; but they should hold up as an example what other socialist countries in the world have given away to the underprivileged people during all the time we have heard of socialism. Their policy is to give everything away until we become one of the underprivileged countries of the world.
We have the international wheat agreement and we have the wheat board. The government has just made a final payment on last year's crop. I think even the socialists will agree that that payment was quite good. However, they are not ready to give the government credit for it. The Minister of Trade and Commerce will not ask for any credit, but the fact is it was a pretty good wheat payment. If it was more than the average producer expected, and I think it was; if the government is to receive no credit for it, then why should the government be faced with a political implication that it has not acted as it should when the final payment is a few cents less than was expected?

They asked the people to vote against the wheat steal. That is a contribution the socialists made during the by-election in Gravelbourg a year and a half ago. Vote against the wheat steal. Mr. Speaker, I should like to add my plea to that made by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw) the other night when he asked for some changes to be made in the Prairie Farm Assistance Act as it applies to hail benefits. Under the present six-section eligibility clause we find that we have a great deal of discrimination. It is not deliberate discrimination; but with hail acting in the way it does, it cannot be helped. It is almost impossible to administer an act such as the Prairie Farm Assistance Act unless there is some reduction in the eligibility clause. All westerners know that hail is extremely unpredictable. At times you will have a narrow strip where the hail will cut a swathe many miles long. At other times it will hit one farm, skip one and hit another. This phenomenon makes it extremely difficult, if not impossible, to administer the act as it should be administered. The only real solution to this problem would be found if the hail benefits were to be reduced to an individual basis. If the government is not willing to do that-that is, bring it down to the individual basis-they should at least bring it down to a one-section basis so the farmers who are suffering hail damage will not be discriminated against.

I cannot understand why the government and the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation insist on spending the taxpayers' money to do a job that private concerns are willing to do with no cost at all to the Canadian taxpayers. As a matter of fact the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation set $1 million as the cost of a television station on the west coast, where private companies have claimed that they can set one up for as little as $500,000.

They have that type of thing in Russia, but there is no place for it in a democratic country such as ours. If the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is to be the controlling body for television and radio, then it should get out of circulation as a competing body; or if it is going to be the competing body, then let us set up some other body to control both radio and television. Mr. Speaker, at the beginning of each session the speech from the throne informs parliament of the matters that will be discussed and forecasts the legislation to be enacted for the good of the country. The speech contains wide, general and sometimes vague statements. One must read between the lines to find out exactly what legislation is proposed. The wider the meaning, the greater opportunity it affords of debating the various aspects of our national problems. This year the speech places before us such important matters as international policy, the St. Lawrence seaway project, radio television, international trade, and so forth. Before expressing an opinion on one or two of those problems which are so important to Canadians I should like to add my congratulations to

The Address

Mr. Boisvert those already offered to the mover of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, the hon. member for Brome-Missis-quoi (Mr. Deslieres) and to the seconder, the hon. member for Waterloo North (Mr. Schneider) upon the manner in which they have discharged a difficult task. They have won the admiration of this house and have fully justified the confidence placed in them by the electors of their respective constituencies.
I should like also to congratulate the two hon. gentlemen who have been appointed members of the government. I refer to the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Campney) who is an Associate Minister of National Defence and the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair) who is our new Minister of Fisheries. I have no doubt that both of these gentlemen will carry out their duties with competence and with the highest standards of responsibility.
I want to extend a welcome to our new colleagues the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin) and the hon. member for Outremont-St. Jean (Mr. Bourque). Their presence in this chamber is evidence that hon. members opposite are in a brown study if they think the Liberal party has lost any of its strength in the province of Quebec. (Translation):
Now, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words in my mother tongue about a matter that has already been dealt with by the hon. members for Labelle (Mr. Court-emanche) and for Portneuf (Mr. Gauthier). It is about a great Canadian, Mr. Henri Bourassa. In doing so, I must not forget that one of his friends, Mr. Paul-Emile Lamarche, was member for Nicolet-Yamaska from 1911 to 1917 and I should also recall to the house that Mr. Paul-Emile Lamarche was always true to Mr. Bourassa.
As I said a moment ago, the hon. members for Labelle and for Portneuf paid a well-deserved tribute to Mr. Bourassa. At the turn of the century, I was too young to accept or reject Mr. Bourassa's ideas. However I had occasion to meet him during the course of my legal practice and I always had much admiration and sympathy for his wide talent and his spirited oratory. He was a dangerous politician and he will be remembered.
A friend of Laurier, he fought against him and then made friends again. He deserves that we honour his memory, that we remember him as a man of exceptional culture, constantly inspired by a strong desire to clash with someone on the ideological field.
In the course of the last debates in which he took part, he voted against the party to which the hon. member for Labelle is quite

proud and happy to belong. I am sorry that he is not in his seat tonight. On a matter of great interest, trade relations between Great Britain and the commonwealth, Mr. Bourassa spoke as follows, on May 15, 1930. I quote from page 2127 of Hansard:
"I sympathize with the English, I think the world would be worse if England disappeared, the world would suffer if English power were too greatly weakened. However, it is ridiculous, it is the thought of a parvenu or of a child who has not measured his strength, to imagine that we can settle the affairs of England. Let us rather come back to the thought which has been frequently expressed by the leader of this government and by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe): Let us frame our policy first to suit ourselves, but frame it with an open eye, so that we may deal preferentially with people who are prepared to deal with us. I wish to state that there is no people on earth with whom I would rather deal, or with whom I would rather commune mentally or politically, than the British people.
At this very moment, the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. St. Laurent) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) are in England where they are attending a conference which will deal with problems similar to those we had to face in 1930. There is no doubt, on this side of the house, that our representatives will take stands consistent with the best traditions of our party and in the best interest of our country. We do not see very well how our relations with Great Britain and the nations of the commonwealth could affect our actual sovereignty and the authority of our parliament over our own affairs as a nation. It is difficult to understand what the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) meant when he said, during the present debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, as reported on page 28 of Hansard:
Our real sovereignty and full authority over our own affairs as a nation will depend in very large measure on the extent to which the Canadian government succeeds in reopening the commonwealth and sterling markets so that our trade is better balanced, and we have some freedom of action in the event of economic storms in the United States or acting at any time by their government which might interrupt the flow of our exports. There is nothing in the speech from the throne to indicate any intention on the part of the government to take appropriate action in pursuance of this great need.
It is strange that the Leader of the Opposition could have spoken of centralization in connection with relations between the government and the provinces, when, in his opinion, our sovereignty as a nation would be threatened if we failed to resume trade relations with England and the commonwealth countries. Does it mean that our sovereignty is still

partly dependent on Great Britain? If that were the case, it would be imperative for the hon. member from Labelle to shed his Harlequin's coat. His nationalism is closely akin to that of those who betrayed Bourassa and of whom he complained all his life. (Text):
I should like to deal with some of the international problems. What emerges most strikingly from the speech from the throne, the terms, aspects and forecasts of which we are now studying, are policies both national and international. There are very few questions which are not in one way or another linked up with the unsettled and threatening international situation. Certain problems which seem to be of a purely local economic nature become interwoven with conditions that arise in distant or neighbouring countries. For instance, the outbreak of the foot-and-mouth disease was a local affair, but that was followed by an embargo imposed by the government of the United States which made inoperative for a time a trade agreement of international character.
Canada was blessed with a bumper crop this year, but our western farmers will not benefit unless it is disposed of in the markets of the world under our trade agreements. Again this is a matter of policy at the international level.
I have already stated that in the international field the situation is confused, uncertain and even gloomy. The Korean war does not seem to have given rise, in so far as the democratic countries are concerned, to an emotional reaction which would cause this struggle to be considered by the people involved as a holy war, one which falls well within the terms of the first paragraph of article 1 of the United Nations charter signed at San Francisco on June 26, 1945. This article reads as follows:
The purposes ot the United Nations are:
1. To maintain international peace and security, and to that end: to take effective collective measures for the prevention and removal of threats to peace, and for the suppression of acts of aggression or other breaches of the peace, and to bring about by peaceful means, and in conformity with the principles of justice and international law, adjustment or settlement of international disputes or situations which might lead to a breach of the peace.
When the United Nations charter was signed a wave of confidence swept over the world. It seemed to us all that at last the whole globe would be delivered from the nightmare of war and that the peoples of the world, having walked a bloody path for so long, would at length understand how to adapt civilization to modern conditions, would be capable of establishing an international sovereignty based on a peaceful rule of law,
The Address-Mr. Boisvert with no recourse to armaments more shocking and terrifying than the fires of heaven. Yet, unfortunately, nothing has changed except for the worse. Russia, thanks to its communist agents, has managed to bring into its sphere of influence, through devious means incorporating blackmail and threats, would-be free nations such as Poland, Czechoslovakia, Bulgaria and Roumania, to speak of Europe. In Asia we have China, this inexhaustible reservoir of human beings whose poverty and fatalism may in time make possible the formation of immense armies ready to undertake violent wars of conquest at Russia's behest in the name of that materialistic ideology which, so to speak, divorces the human spirit from its true function, which is thought, and weds it instead to a doctrine of blind animal subservience. The docility and servility of these armies would turn them into instruments of mass murder and destruction.
For the past two years Asia Minor and Africa have been shaken by a series of disquieting events. This brings us to the Iranian oil question, the question of treaties between England and Egypt, the uprising of the negroes in Kenya, the racial question in South Africa. I say these things to show that, from the point of view of international strategy, the area of the territories where large-scale manoeuvres could be undertaken to bring about the victory of our armies is more and more narrowing, more and more shrinking. If Russia, through its agents urging the indigenous population of African countries to revolt, succeeded in putting the political, economic and military situation of our allies and the member states of the North Atlantic treaty in a precarious position should war break out anew, which heaven forbid, then it will be possible to win it only by the virtual obliteration of the enemies of the liberty and security of all peoples, a solution that would annihilate more than half the globe. It means that we would have to use atomic bombs as well as the hydrogen bomb, whose unavoidable use would be equivalent to a real betrayal of our civilization. As between losing and winning, of course we will have to win, but at what a shameful price.
In the face of this pessimistic view of things, I wonder whether it would not be advisable to revise the international policy of free peoples and revert to secret diplomacy rather than this open diplomacy which has been practised since the last war. We well realize that the meetings of the United Nations are a forum for Moscow-inspired diplomats. They are thus in a position to

The Address-Mr. Boisvert submerge the whole world, as they do indeed, with their insidious and skilful propaganda. So far as our side is concerned, Russia by all means conceivable, as much within its own borders as beyond those of satellite countries, prevents the diplomats of the member nations of the North Atlantic treaty from reciprocating by informing their nationals of the objectives which we intend to achieve in order to maintain universal order in an atmosphere of peaceful stability, and in adopting for this purpose only amicable solutions liable to produce earnest advantages for all peace loving and progressive peoples. As long as the United Nations are serving the objectives of Russia and communism in the world, would it not be better to rely on a much more secret diplomacy which would plunge Russian diplomats and Russophiles into perplexity as regards our means, and leave the Russian people in a troublesome anxiety?
Is it not true that controversies break out here and there within the member nations of the North Atlantic pact to the effect that the United Nations is not able to achieve the end it had in view? It seems also that the Korean war will not be settled by the general assembly of the United Nations, as it appears that the meetings of the United Nations are becoming a source of conflict between member nations. France, for instance, complains bitterly of the stand taken by the United States on the claims made by the people of Tunisia and Morocco. The United Nations meetings are truly marathons of oratory by the Russians and advocates of the so-called people's democracies, who stir up throughout the world a kind of propaganda which is likely to push farther and farther back the horizon where, at one point, it appeared to us that the star of peace had risen in a sky still red with the fires of destruction. Russia and communism profit considerably by our divisions and our disagreements which, however normal and understandable they may be, show that notwithstanding our efforts toward peace we are far from seeing eye to eye on the means of attaining it.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) deserves to be complimented on his appointment to the general assembly of the United Nations. His appointment reflects the position our country occupies among the nations of the world, and it shows up the personality of our Secretary of State for External Affairs, a personality which is acknowledged by the government of Canada, the House of Commons and the Canadian people. The Secretary of State for External Affairs wants peace. If he does not attain it

we shall know where to put the blame, for he will waste no opportunity to make use of his ability and wisdom in order to find and have accepted a formula which will respect the rights based on international justice. The Secretary of State for External Affairs is not far from the views I have just expressed when, in the foreword to the book "Canada and the United Nations, 1951-1952" he writes:
The United Nations is neither a military alliance against communism nor an embryonic form of world government. Essentially the charter of the United Nations is a multilateral treaty which has been ratified by the great majority of sovereign states. It is a treaty with enormous scope and has led to the establishment of machinery for nearly every form of international political, social, economic, cultural and humanitarian co-operation. Yet it is a treaty which is meant specifically to protect the jurisdiction of states in essentially domestic matters. Moreover, it is a treaty which in collective security matters requires for its full enforcement unanimity among the great powers. Not only does this unanimity not exist; there is acute division between these powers-between the free world and the Soviet world. The United Nations did not create this division but it does reflect it.
In view of the fact that the United Nations seems unable to reach our objective of peace without taking the risk of being involved in a general conflict, it might be wiser to revert to ancient diplomacy and try to ward off war by a web of military defensive alliances. These alliances would see nations bind themselves through clauses similar to article 5 of the North Atlantic treaty which reads as follows:
The parties agree that an armed attack against one or more of them in Europe or North America shall be considered an attack against them all; and consequently they agree that, if such an armed attack occurs, each of them, in exercise of the right of individual or collective self-defence recognized by article 51 of the charter of the United Nations, will assist the party or parties so attacked by taking forthwith, individually and in concert with the other parties, such action as it deems necessary, including the use of armed force, to restore and maintain the security of the North Atlantic area.
The North Atlantic treaty will undoubtedly become the stumbling block on the road to peace because, under this treaty, in order to deter aggression rather than as a menace to Russia and her satellites, the member nations are engaged in building military strength capable of holding in check any possible enemy who might be tempted to infringe the security of the United Nations or threaten their territorial integrity. In order to reinforce the clauses of the treaty, multilateral pacts should be signed, even between nations who are parties to the North Atlantic treaty and their immediate neighbours. Such treaties could be arranged between groups of Asiatic, African or South American nations which would, at a later

date, become part of the North Atlantic alliance. This would ensure that the clauses of the United Nations charter would become the law of all nations.
The study of diplomacy shows us that offensive and defensive military treaties did not prevent the wars of 1914 and 1939. Let us not forget, however, that the parties to those alliances were separated by other countries which demanded that their neutrality be respected by their neighbours. Because of these neutrality agreements, the nation which was ready to wage a war and hoped to turn its aggression to the best advantage has always attacked one or other of these "neutral" countries which had fondly believed that it would not be engulfed in a conflict or become victim of an invasion. Once disarmed, these nations were easy prey. This neutrality was one of the reasons the military agreements remained ineffective. The signing of agreements similar to the North Atlantic treaty between groups of two or three adjoining nations would ensure a more effective defence of their territory, and offer a salient of resistance which would permit the forces set up by the members of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization to rush to the rescue of the country which might be attacked or invaded directly by Russia or her satellites. Mr. Heeney, Canada's permanent representative to the North Atlantic council, in a speech at Oxford on September 10, 1952, made the following statement, which I quote from the External Affairs Bulletin of October, 1952, page 342 of the English edition:
Now it is true, of course, that our fourteen nations have much in common beyond our determination to remain free and to build up our strength to deter, and, if need be, to fight together against aggression. But, if it is difficult to delimit in terms of strategy the extent of our community, how much more difficult is it to set geographical boundaries to the spiritual community of free men?
I am not suggesting that there is no essential unity, no political or other logic in the present grouping of nations in NATO. Much less am I suggesting that NATO should put on a drive for new members! Of course the present composition of the alliance makes sense-but it is primarily military sense at the present stage of events. All that I am trying to say is that we should remember that NATO does not comprise the whole community of free men. And we should look forward to the widening, as well as the deepening, of our association, particularly in those fields of endeavour associated with article 2 of the treaty which, in NATO parlance, have come to be known as the "non-military aspects".
I shall go further. If a war is in the making by the enemies of freedom, the whole community of free peoples should be militarily organized, not to launch an attack but to defend itself more effectively. The nations which have become conscious of their ability
The Address-Mr. Boisvert to resist aggression may want to avail themselves increasingly of the provisions of article 2 of the North Atlantic treaty concerning peaceful and friendly international relations. It is impossible to stabilize free institutions when people are living in a state of uncertainty and insecurity.
War itself must be looked upon as an institution. Mythology had a god of war. Mankind, since it has been able to form groups and societies, has always waged war and, alas, always had to bear it. There have been racial and religious wars, wars of conquest and revenge, slave wars and so forth. Even the most developed civilizations could not stop them, and it must be granted that the more men have been policed and civilized, the more wars have destroyed lives, wealth, cities and countries. Before our Christian era conquerors took prisoners and put them into slavery. In more recent times prisoners have been taken and put into concentration camps to die, or been subjected to experiments that are loathsome to the mind. Were the mass slaughters practised in China thousands of years before Christ more inhuman than the executions that took place during the last great war? If war itself is an institution then it should be dealt with as such, especially when we know that a nation or a group of nations takes pleasure in creating situations and difficulties that may cause an outbreak at any moment.
Multifarious military alliances would make nations, great and small, more realistic about their security and their governments would be less inclined to rely on the armies of America to safeguard their territorial integrity. There is great danger of the people of America being led to believe that they will be the sole guardians of peace and security for the western bloc of nations. Our economic power is acting as a sedative on many European individuals. If nations that we have undertaken to protect and to defend were unable to offer the least resistance in case of an invasion, our armies on the spot could be destroyed far from their homeland, our own means of defence would be weakened, and our people would have to endure a siege of aerial war that could last a long time. There exists such a trend in United States policy. I can see this trend in connection with the Korean war. A well-known Republican representative, Joseph W. Martin, Jr., of Massachusetts, declared during a recent interview:
We must waste no time in building up the anticommunist forces in Asia. We have got to build up the Korean army so that our boys can be withdrawn from the front line. I think we should build up the Japanese forces to deter aggression and we should encourage rebellions on the mainland of China.

The Address-Mr. Boisvert
I do not agree with the last part of Mr. Martin's statement because under the principle of self-determination for nations and peoples, they must be free to adopt the means they find proper to avoid and to defeat aggression. It would be a mistake on the part of United States diplomacy to make itself the agent of revolutions and rebellions. This would irritate the Chinese masses and enlarge the gap between Asiatic and American thought. On the other hand, if we could set up a Korean army with sufficient power to end the conflict and, at the same time, to bring home our troops, this would be a great step toward ensuring a better understanding between Asia, Europe and America.
From the moment he assumed command of the United Nations troops in Korea, General Van Fleet turned his activity in that direction. He has recruited young Koreans, and has instructed and trained them with great success. Korean soldiers proved equal to ours during the recent fighting to hold the hills. The presence of United Nations soldiers in Asia was necessary. However, one should not try to hide the fact that hundreds of millions of individuals consider it rather as a symbol of territorial claims rather than a move to defeat an unjust aggression. The United Nations army looks as though it were starting on a conquest of Asia where, according to Russian and Chinese propaganda, we are imposing by force our way of life, our ideas, etc. In time it would become possible, through the efforts of skilful diplomacy, to bring the populations of Asia to live in peace with one another and with ourselves, and to have relations with Europe and America which would, little by little, rescue them from the influence of Moscow.
I have not lost faith in the United Nations. We must not, either, lose faith in the efforts made by the general assembly of the United Nations to bring about a better understanding among all the nations of the world, among nations and peoples of different religions and races. There is much to be expected from what is going on in Europe. For the first time in history, France, Germany and Italy, to mention only the principal nations which have adopted the Schuman plan, have agreed to pool their resources of coal and steel to ensure a better distribution; for this has been the cause, in the past, of many conflicts. Another step is being made with a constituent assembly of Europe organizing itself to form a true European community with supranational powers granted by the states which
will join that new and unique community of nations.
Freedom is one and indivisible; it exists for all human beings wherever they happen to live by reason of their birth. To retain its value, freedom requires a peaceful atmosphere. Such an atmosphere will exist only when war has been defeated. It is the spirit which prevailed in 1945 at the signing of the charter of the United Nations. The principles enunciated in the charter of the United Nations cannot be too often reiterated; and it is important for all of us to seek to bring about, at long last, the state of things which should exist, and then to ensure a lasting peace for the world at any cost whatever, be it money or gold. Gold and money can be recovered, but human lives cannot be restored.
Dark as may appear the sky under which the sessions of the general assembly of the United Nations are being held, one must share the views which were recently expressed by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) in the following terms:
After seven years the United Nations is still a young organization, still largely an experiment. But one thing has become increasingly evident. Despite the disappointments we have all encountered, there is no doubt that the spirit of interdependence in the world is growing . . . The progress is slow, but it is in the right direction and is constantly being made, often in the United Nations bodies which receive very little publicity. We must not, then, think of the United Nations solely in terms of the bitter disputes which now loom so large in the headlines. Our hope for the future of our world organization has a deeper and more solid foundation than these headlines would suggest. The battle against ignorance and prejudice and, yes, even against fear is steadily and perseveringly being fought. It must continue until one day victory is achieved.
I wish I could have expressed opinions on the question of radio television, the St. Lawrence seaway project and federal-provincial relations. I am sure we shall be given the opportunity to do so during the debates which will follow on those matters of great interest that will, of course, influence the progress and development of our country toward a destiny which we want all nations to envy and which should be based on law, justice, broad-mindedness, mutual understanding and, above all, respect of the human person and dignity.
